Grammar: Accents

French uses 4 accent marks that change pronunciation:

1. Accent aigu (é) — acute accent, sounds like "ay"
Example: é in "café" = kah-FAY

2. Accent grave (è) — grave accent, sounds like "eh" (more open)
Example: è in "mère" = MEHR

3. Cédille (ç) — soft 's' sound before a/o/u
Example: ç in "français" = franss-AY (not frank-AY)

4. Tréma (ï) — keeps two vowels as separate sounds
Example: maïs (corn) — mah-EE (not rhymes with "but")

French uses accent marks that change pronunciation.
Accent aigu (é) — acute accent.
Accent grave (è) — grave accent.
Cédille (ç) — turns a "c" before a/o/u into a soft "s" sound instead of a hard "k" sound.
Tréma (ï) — shows two vowels next to each other are pronounced separately, not blended into one sound.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
francaisfrançaisMissing cédille changes pronunciation from "franss-ay" to "frank-ay"
mais (thinking corn)maïsWithout tréma, sounds like "but" (one blended vowel). With tréma, sounds like "corn" (two separate vowels)
cafecaféMissing accent aigu. "Cafe" sounds flat; "café" has the proper "ay" sound
meremèreMissing accent grave. Affects pronunciation of the vowel

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: français (French language/person)

The cédille makes it "franss-ay" instead of "frank-ay". Critical pronunciation difference!

Example 2: maïs (corn)

The tréma keeps "a" and "i" as two separate sounds (mah-EE). Without it, it's "mais" meaning "but".

Example 3: café (coffee/café)

The accent aigu (é) makes it sound like "kah-FAY". A common word you'll use often!

Example 4: François (a common French name)

Shows cédille in a real name. You'll hear this name often in French contexts.

💬 Natural Conversation

Emma: Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Emma. (Hello! My name's Emma.)
Léo: Enchanté, Emma ! Comment ça s'écrit ? (Nice to meet you, Emma! How's that spelled?)
Emma: E, M, M, A. Et toi, comment tu t'appelles ? (E-M-M-A. And you, what's your name?)
Léo: Je m'appelle Léo. (My name's Léo.)

How to count 20–69 in French

Build numbers using the tens plus units. Key pattern: use 'et' only with 1:

  • 20 = vingt
  • 21 = vingt et un (with 'et')
  • 22 = vingt-deux (no 'et')
  • 30 = trente
  • 40 = quarante
  • 50 = cinquante
  • 60 = soixante

Numbers: 70–99 (Tricky French Number System)

The special French number system

  • 70 = 60 + 10 → soixante-dix
  • 80 = 4 × 20 → quatre-vingt
  • 90 = (4 × 20) + 10 → quatre-vingt-dix

Rule for "et":
Soixante et onze (71 has "et")
Quatre-vingt-un (81 has NO "et")

Days of the Week

Quel est le premier jour de la semaine ? — What is the first day of the week?
Réponse: Le premier jour de la semaine est lundi — The first day of the week is Monday.

Quels sont les 7 jours de la semaine ? — What are the 7 days of the week?

1. Lundi = Monday
2. Mardi = Tuesday
3. Mercredi = Wednesday
4. Jeudi = Thursday
5. Vendredi = Friday
6. Samedi = Saturday
7. Dimanche = Sunday

Important: In French, the first day of the week is Monday, not Sunday! Days are lowercase and not usually preceded by "le" in sentences.

Asking the Time

Two ways to ask the time

  • Quelle heure est-il ? (most common)
  • Quelle heure fait-il ? (alternate form)

Both mean "What time is it?" Learn both forms to understand them when spoken.

Gender Agreement in Numbers

Un/une agree with the noun's gender

  • 41 (masculine) → quarante et un
  • 41 minutes (feminine) → quarante et une minutes
  • 41 cars (feminine) → quarante et une voitures

The gender form depends on the noun being counted, not just the number.

Duration example

C'est deux heures et demie de route. — It's two and a half hours of driving.
C'est deux heures et trente minutes de route. — Same meaning, said differently.
une demi-heure — half an hour

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Il est 2h30 et quartIl est 2h45 (or 3h moins le quart)Et quart means quarter (15 min), not 45 min. 45 min = moins le quart (quarter to the next hour).
Il est demi heuresIl est deux heures et demieSay "et demie" (with feminine agreement) after the hour. "Demi" must agree: demie (feminine) before the noun.
Quelle est l'heure?Quelle heure est-il? (or Quelle heure fait-il?)Use "Quelle heure est-il?" not "Quelle est l'heure?" (though both work, the first is more standard).
Il est 14 heures et demiIl est 14 heures et demie (or 2h30 de l'après-midi)"Demie" is feminine and agrees with "heure". Must use "demie" not "demi".
Il est trois heures moins un quartIl est trois heures moins le quartUse "le quart" (the quarter) not just "un quart" when saying time.

💬 Natural Conversation

Sophie: Salut Marc ! On se voit demain ? (Hi Marc! Shall we meet tomorrow?)
Marc: Oui ! Quelle heure te convient ? (Yes! What time works for you?)
Sophie: Trois heures et quart, ça va ? (Quarter past three, does that work?)
Marc: Parfait, à demain alors ! (Perfect, see you tomorrow then!)

Les Groupes de Verbes — Comment Les Reconnaître — Foundational

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: How to correctly identify which of the 3 French verb groups a new verb belongs to — the key skill for tackling any verb you haven't memorized yet.

0 / 4 done
This is the chapter to come back to whenever you meet a new verb and aren't sure how to conjugate it. Knowing the group tells you which pattern to apply.

1️⃣ The 3 Groups — Overview

GroupRuleExamples
1er groupeinfinitive ends in -ER (except aller)parler, manger, habiter, aimer
2e groupeinfinitive ends in -IR AND present participle ends in -ISSANTfinir, choisir, grandir
3e groupeeverything else: all -RE, all -OIR, irregular -IR (no -issant), aller, être, avoir, fairevendre, voir, partir, venir, aller
The 1st group is by far the biggest — roughly 90% of French verbs are regular -ER verbs. If a new verb ends in -er and isn't aller, it's almost certainly 1st group and regular.

2️⃣ The -ISSANT Test — Telling 2nd Group from Irregular -IR Verbs

Test: does "en ___issant" sound like a real word? If yes → 2nd group. If no → 3rd group (irregular, learn individually).
Verb"en ___issant"?Group
finiren finissant ✓ sounds right2nd — regular
choisiren choisissant ✓ sounds right2nd — regular
partir"en partissant" ✗ not a word (it's en partant)3rd — irregular
venir"en venissant" ✗ not a word (it's en venant)3rd — irregular
ouvrir"en ouvrissant" ✗ not a word (it's en ouvrant)3rd — irregular
This is the single most common mix-up: NOT all -ir verbs behave alike. Always run the -issant test before assuming a verb is 2nd group.

3️⃣ Aller: The Big -ER Exception

Aller (to go) ends in -er just like parler — but it does NOT conjugate the same way at all:

  • ❌ "j'alle" — this is NOT how aller works
  • ✓ je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont — completely irregular
Memorize this one by sight: aller is the single most common verb whose ending "lies" about its group.

Présent : Verbes du 1er Groupe (-ER) — Foundational

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: Regular -ER verbs in the present tense — ~90% of all French verbs — including the silent-endings trick and the three common spelling quirks (-GER, -CER, -ELER/-ETER).

0 / 5 done
Master this one pattern and you can conjugate the vast majority of French verbs. This is the single highest-value lesson in the whole site.

1️⃣ The Rule

Base: infinitive minus -ER, plus: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent
Personparler (to speak)
jeje parle
tutu parles
il / elleil/elle parle
nousnous parlons
vousvous parlez
ils / ellesils/elles parlent

2️⃣ 🎯 The Silent-Endings Trick

je, tu, il/elle, and ils/elles — four of six forms — sound IDENTICAL. The -e, -es, and -ent endings are all silent. Say it out loud: parle, parles, parle, parlent — same sound. Only nous (-ons) and vous (-ez) actually sound different. For speaking and listening (both tested on the TCF), you really only need to distinguish 3 sounds, not 6 forms — most of the "memorizing" is spelling, not sound.

3️⃣ Spelling Quirks

Same underlying pattern — these are small spelling adjustments to preserve pronunciation:

TypeRuleExample
-GER (manger, voyager, nager)add extra "e" before -onsnous mangeons, not "mangons"
-CER (commencer, lancer, placer)c → ç before -onsnous commençons, not "commencons"
-ELER / -ETER (appeler, jeter)double the consonant in 4 of 6 forms (not nous/vous)j'appelle, tu appelles, il appelle, ils appellent — but nous appelons, vous appelez
A few -eler/-eter verbs use an accent instead of doubling (acheter → j'achète) — but doubling is the more common pattern. Same logic with jeter: je jette, tu jettes, il jette, ils jettent, but nous jetons, vous jetez.

Grammar: Subject Pronouns

Subject pronouns are words that replace a noun when they do an action or are at the beginning of a sentence.

For example: Instead of saying "Jean is tall" → we say "He is tall"

In French, we have 6 subject pronouns: each one changes depending on who does the action and affects how we conjugate verbs.

This is one of the most important concepts in French!

1. Je (I) — Used when talking about yourself
Example: Je suis étudiant = I am a student

2. Tu (you - informal) — With friends, family
Example: Tu es gentil = You are kind

3. Il / Elle (he / she) — Il for boys, Elle for girls
Example: Il est français = He is French

4. Nous (we) — For groups
Example: Nous sommes amis = We are friends

5. Vous (you - formal/plural) — Teachers, bosses, plural
Example: Vous êtes professeur = You are a teacher

6. Ils / Elles (they) — Ils for boys/mixed, Elles for girls
Example: Ils sont étudiants = They are students

The subject pronoun comes at the beginning of a sentence before the verb. It tells us WHO does the action.

Examples:

Je parle = I speak
Tu danses = You dance
Elle chante = She sings
Nous courons = We run

Important: The verb changes based on the pronoun used. This is called conjugation.

Memorize how each verb changes for each pronoun!

Tu vs Vous (The Most Important Distinction!):

Tu = Informal (You with friends/family)

Used with: friends, family, classmates, people your age
Creates a friendly, personal atmosphere
Example: Tu es mon ami = You are my friend (to a close friend)

Vous = Formal/Respectful (You with strangers/authority)

Used with: teachers, boss, grandparents, strangers, people you want to show respect to
Also used when talking to multiple people (even friends!)
Example: Vous êtes professeur = You are a teacher (to your teacher)

⚠️ Cultural Note: Using Tu with someone you just met can seem rude. Using Vous with close friends can seem too formal. Getting this right is crucial in French society!

FrenchEnglish
jeI
tuyou (informal)
il / ellehe / she
nouswe
vousyou (formal / plural)
ils / ellesthey

Vocabulary: Times of the Day

1. Le matin (Morning) — from sunrise to noon
Example: Je vais à l'école le matin = I go to school in the morning

2. Midi (Noon) — exactly 12 o'clock
Example: Je mange à midi = I eat at noon

3. L'après-midi (Afternoon) — from noon to evening
Example: On se voit l'après-midi = We see each other in the afternoon

4. Le soir (Evening) — from late afternoon until nighttime
Example: Je suis fatigué le soir = I am tired in the evening

5. Minuit (Midnight) — exactly 12 o'clock at night
Example: Minuit est l'heure du silence = Midnight is the hour of silence

6. La nuit (Night) — from evening until sunrise
Example: Je dors la nuit = I sleep at night

Vocabulary: Common Greetings

In the morning (le matin): Use Bonjour to greet, and when leaving say Bonne journée = Have a nice day

At noon (midi): Still use Bonjour, and you can say Bon appétit before eating

In the afternoon (l'après-midi): Use Bonjour or Bon après-midi = Good afternoon

In the evening (le soir): Use Bonsoir = Good evening, and when leaving say Bonne soirée = Have a nice evening

At night (la nuit): When going to bed, say Bonne nuit = Good night

Important: Never say Bonsoir before 5-6pm — that's too early! Always use Bonjour before evening.

FrenchEnglish
Bonjour !Hello! / Good morning!
Bonne journée !Have a nice day!
Bon après-midi !Good afternoon!
Bonsoir !Good evening!
Bonne soirée !Have a nice evening!
Bonne nuit !Good night!

Vocabulary: Formal Greetings (vous)

Use formal greetings with: Teachers, bosses, strangers, older people, anyone you want to show respect to

Greeting forms:

Bonjour madame = Hello, ma'am (to a woman)
Bonjour mademoiselle = Hello, miss (to an unmarried young woman)
Bonjour monsieur = Hello, sir (to a man)

Asking how they are:

Comment allez-vous ? = How are you? (formal)
Vous allez bien ? = Are you doing well?
Et vous ? = And you? (after they tell you about themselves)

Important: Always use vous with strangers and authority figures. Never use tu unless they tell you to!

FrenchEnglish

Bonjour mademoiselle !Good morning/Hello, miss!
Bonsoir monsieur !Good evening, sir!
Comment allez-vous ?How are you?
Vous allez bien ?Are you doing well?
Et vous ?And you?

Vocabulary: Informal Greetings (tu)

Use informal greetings with: Friends, family, classmates, people your age, close acquaintances

Greeting forms:

Bonjour or Salut = Hello (friendly)
Coucou = Hi there! (very casual and warm)

Asking how they are:

Ça va ? = How's it going? (most casual)
Comment ça va ? = How are you?
Comment vas-tu ? = How are you? (more structured)
Tu vas bien ? = Are you doing well?
Et toi ? = And you? (after they answer)

Important: Use tu to create warmth and closeness. It shows you value the friendship or relationship!

Grammar: Être (to be) — present tense

Use être to say: Who you are, where you from, what profession you have, how you feel, or to describe a state

Conjugation in present tense:

Je suis = I am
Tu es = You are
Il/Elle est = He/She is
Nous sommes = We are
Vous êtes = You are (formal/plural)
Ils/Elles sont = They are

Examples:
Je suis français = I am French
Tu es étudiant = You are a student
Elle est ici = She is here
Nous sommes amis = We are friends

Grammar: Avoir (to have) — present tense

Use avoir to say: What you own/possess, your age (using "j'ai X ans"), how you feel (hunger, luck, cold, fear), or to describe possession

Conjugation in present tense:

J'ai = I have
Tu as = You have
Il/Elle a = He/She has
Nous avons = We have
Vous avez = You have (formal/plural)
Ils/Elles ont = They have

Examples:
J'ai un livre = I have a book
Tu as une voiture = You have a car
Elle a 25 ans = She is 25 years old (literally: She has 25 years)
Nous avons faim = We are hungry (literally: We have hunger)
J'ai de la chance = I am lucky (literally: I have luck)

Note: This is an IRREGULAR verb — memorize all six forms! And remember: French uses avoir for age and emotions!

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Tu es mon ami (to a stranger)Vous êtes mon amiUse TU only with friends/family. Use VOUS with strangers or authority figures
Comment tu vas (very formal)Ça va?Use formal "Comment allez-vous?" or casual "Ça va?" Never mix informality incorrectly
Je ai un livreJ'ai un livreAlways use contraction "J'ai" before vowels, not "Je ai"
Il ont 20 ansIl a 20 ansConjugate avoir correctly: "il a" (not "ont"). Use "ils ont" for plural
Bonjour matinBonjour (le matin)"Bonjour" works for any time of day. Use "Bonsoir" only in evening (after dark)

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: Bonjour, comment allez-vous?

Formal greeting to a teacher/boss. "Comment allez-vous" is the respectful version of "how are you?"

Example 2: Ça va bien, et toi?

Casual greeting with a friend. "Et toi" is informal for "and you?" (with friends). Use "Et vous?" formally.

Example 3: J'ai 20 ans

In French, you "have" age (not "are" age). Literally "I have 20 years" = "I am 20 years old"

Example 4: Au revoir, à demain!

Classic goodbye. "À demain" = "See you tomorrow"

Example 5: Vous êtes professeur?

Formal question to ask someone's profession. Always use VOUS when speaking to someone formally.

💬 Natural Conversation

Léo: Salut Emma, ça va ? (Hey Emma, how's it going?)
Emma: Ça va bien, merci ! Et toi, comment vas-tu ? (I'm doing well, thanks! And you, how are you?)
Léo: Très bien aussi. Bon, je dois y aller. (Very well too. Well, I have to go.)
Emma: D'accord, à bientôt ! (Okay, see you soon!)

Grammar: Pronominal verbs — s'appeler

Pronominal verbs are verbs whose infinitive starts with se (reflexive — the action reflects back on the subject).

s'appeler — literally "to call oneself", used to say your name.

Conjugation:

je m'appelle = my name is (I call myself)
tu t'appelles = your name is (you call yourself)
il/elle s'appelle = his/her name is (he/she calls himself/herself)
nous nous appelons = our names are (we call ourselves)
vous vous appelez = your names are (you call yourselves)
ils/elles s'appellent = their names are (they call themselves)

Examples:
Je m'appelle Arthur = My name is Arthur
Tu t'appelles Marie = Your name is Marie
Il s'appelle Jean = His name is Jean

Important: The reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) always comes before the verb!

il / elles'appelle
nousnous appelons
vousvous appelez

Grammar: Aller (to go) — present tense

Aller means to go and is used constantly to say where you are going and what you will do.

Conjugation in present tense:

Il/Elle va = He/She goes
Nous allons = We go
Vous allez = You go (formal/plural)
Ils/Elles vont = They go

Examples:
Je vais à l'école = I go to school
Tu vas au parc = You go to the park
Elle va à la maison = She goes home

Note: Aller is COMPLETELY IRREGULAR! Memorize all six forms. Also used for near future: Je vais parler = I am going to speak

Classroom Survival Phrases

What are classroom survival phrases?

These are essential expressions you use in a French classroom to handle common situations. They help you ask for clarification, apologize for lateness, request repetition, and ask how to say something in French. Using proper politeness forms (tu vs vous) shows respect and helps you communicate effectively.

Vocabulary: Classroom survival phrases

FrenchEnglish
Comment ça s'écrit ?How do you spell it?
Vous pouvez répéter s'il vous plaît ?Can you repeat, please?
s'il vous plaîtplease (formal)
s'il te plaîtplease (informal)
Excusez-moi, je suis en retard.Excuse me, I'm late.
Je ne comprends pas.I don't understand.
Comment on dit … en français ?How do we say … in French?

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je comprendre pasJe ne comprends pasNegation needs both "ne" AND "pas". "Je comprendre" is wrong conjugation; use "comprends" (present tense).
Peut-tu répéter s'il te plait?Peux-tu répéter s'il te plaît?"Pouvoir" = "peux/peut". Tu = "peux" not "peut" (that's il/elle/on). Also: "plaît" has accent.
Excusez me, je suis tardExcusez-moi, je suis en retard"Excusez-moi" is one word. Say "en retard" (in late), not just "tard".
Comment tu dit "hello" en français?Comment on dit "hello" en français?Use impersonal "on" (one/we) not "tu" in this structure. Also "dit" → "dit" stays same (present 3rd person).
S'il vous plaît parler plus lentementS'il vous plaît, pouvez-vous parler plus lentement?More formal: add verb "pouvez-vous" (can you). Or: "S'il vous plaît, plus lentement" (more slowly).

💬 Natural Conversation

Léa: Excusez-moi, je ne comprends pas cette phrase. (Excuse me, I don't understand this sentence.)
Prof: Pas de souci, je répète. (No worries, I'll repeat it.)
Léa: Merci ! Au fait, comment dit-on “notebook” ? (Thanks! By the way, how do you say “notebook”?)
Prof: On dit “un cahier”. (You say “un cahier”.)

Topic: How to identify noun gender in French by word endings, special cases, and common exceptions.

Why Noun Gender Matters

Every French noun has a gender: masculine or feminine.

This gender affects:

  • Which article you use (le vs la, un vs une)
  • How adjectives agree (grand vs grande)
  • How possessives work (mon vs ma, ton vs ta)
  • Past participles in compound tenses

The gender is often unpredictable, BUT there are patterns! Most word endings follow gender rules that can help you guess correctly.

Feminine Noun Endings

Most common feminine endings:

  • -tion / -ion: Almost ALWAYS feminine
    Examples: la connexion, une option, une décision, une nation, la station
  • -ure: Usually feminine
    Examples: la nature, la voiture, la culture, la couture, la peinture
  • -ade: Usually feminine
    Examples: la promenade, la salade, la cascade, la marmelade
  • -e: Most words ending in -e are feminine
    Examples: la porte, la maison, la vie, la page, la table

Masculine Noun Endings

Most common masculine endings:

  • -ment: Usually masculine
    Examples: le gouvernement, le département, le jugement, le logement, le traitement
  • -age: Usually masculine
    Examples: le village, le fromage, le voyage, le courage, le garage, le bagage
  • -oir: Usually masculine
    Examples: le miroir, le tiroir, le couloir, le devoir
  • -isme: Usually masculine
    Examples: le tourisme, le journalisme, le romantisme, le socialisme

More Endings & Épicène Nouns

More masculine endings:

  • -eau: le bateau (boat), le château (castle)
  • -phone: le téléphone, le microphone
  • -scope: le télescope, le microscope
  • -eur (machines/tools): l'ordinateur (computer), le moteur (engine)

More feminine endings:

  • -té: la liberté (freedom), la beauté (beauty)
  • -ette: la bicyclette (bicycle), la fourchette (fork)
  • -ance / -ence: la différence, la chance
  • -esse: la jeunesse (youth), la tristesse (sadness)

Épicène nouns — same spelling for both genders, only the article changes:
un/une artiste, un/une architecte, un/une journaliste, un/une élève

Special Cases: Words Borrowed from English, Days, Months & Seasons

Words borrowed from English = MASCULINE

  • le week-end (weekend)
  • le parking (parking lot)
  • le sport (sport)
  • le tennis (tennis)
  • le football (soccer)

Days of the week = MASCULINE

  • le lundi (Monday), le mardi (Tuesday), le mercredi (Wednesday)
  • le jeudi (Thursday), le vendredi (Friday)
  • le samedi (Saturday), le dimanche (Sunday)

Months = MASCULINE

  • le janvier, le février, le mars, le avril, le mai, le juin
  • le juillet, le août, le septembre, le octobre, le novembre, le décembre

Seasons = MASCULINE

  • le printemps (spring), l'été (summer)
  • l'automne (autumn), l'hiver (winter)

Common Exceptions: Masculine Words Ending in -e

Masculine words ending in -e (common exceptions):

  • Family: le père (father), le frère (brother)
  • People: le philosophe (philosopher), le poète (poet), l'artiste (artist - can be either)
  • Places: le musée (museum), le lycée (high school), le café (café)
  • Other: le tableau (painting), le carnaval (carnival)

⚠️ Strategy: When learning a new noun, always memorize it with its article (le or la, un or une). Don't rely only on word endings!

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
la gouvernementle gouvernement-ment ending = masculine, always "le" not "la". Feminine -ment nouns are extremely rare.
un decisionune décision-tion ending = feminine. "Décision" = feminine ("une"), not masculine ("un").
la voyagele voyage-age ending = masculine. Always "le voyage" for a trip, never "la voyage".

Tom: Oui, et regarde cette jolie voiture miniature — un souvenir parfait ! (Yes, and look at this pretty miniature car — a perfect souvenir!)
Nina: Bonne idée. Je vais l'acheter pour ma sœur. (Good idea. I'll buy it for my sister.)
Tom: Elle va adorer ! (She's going to love it!)

About Articles and Gender

Articles MUST match noun gender and number.

Example masculine noun: le village (the village) / un village (a village)

Example feminine noun: la ville (the city) / une ville (a city)

You already learned how to identify gender by word endings. Now apply that knowledge to choose the right article!

Definite Articles (le / la / l' / les)

What are definite articles?

Definite articles mean "the" in English and must match the gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) of the noun:

  • LE — masculine singular (le village)
  • LA — feminine singular (la ville)
  • L' — before vowels or mute h (l'homme, l'amie)
  • LES — plural of any gender (les villages, les villes)

Examples: Definite articles

MasculineFemininePlural (either)
le village — the villagela ville — the cityles villages
le pont — the bridgela région — the regionles villes
l'homme — the manl'amie — girlfriendles amis
l'ami — the friendles amies

Indefinite Articles (un / une / des)

What are indefinite articles?

Indefinite articles mean "a" or "an" in English and refer to unspecified nouns. They must match gender and number:

  • UN — masculine singular (un village)
  • UNE — feminine singular (une ville)
  • DES — plural of any gender (des villages, des amies)

Use indefinite articles when mentioning something for the first time or when the noun is not specific.

Examples: Indefinite articles

MasculineFemininePlural (either)
un village — a villageune ville — a citydes villages
un pont — a bridgeune région — a regiondes villes
un homme — a manune amie — a girlfrienddes amis
un ami — a frienddes amies

Partitive Articles (some / any)

What are partitive articles?

Partitive articles mean "some" or "any" and express an unspecified quantity. They're formed by combining 'de' with the definite article:

  • DU — de + le (du pain — some bread)
  • DE LA — de + la (de la viande — some meat)
  • DE L' — de + l' (de l'eau — some water)
  • DES — de + les (des haricots — some beans)

Use partitive articles for uncountable nouns and when referring to an unspecified amount.

Je voudrais du pain. — I would like some bread.
Elle mange du chocolat. — She eats (some) chocolate.
Nous buvons de l'eau minérale. — We drink (some) mineral water.
Il achète de la viande. — He is buying (some) meat.
Elle fait pousser des haricots verts. — She grows green beans.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
un voitureune voiture"Voiture" is feminine (ending in -ure). Use "une", not "un".
l' hommel'hommeUse "l'" (with apostrophe) before vowels, not "l' " (with space). "Homme" starts with vowel sound.
Je voudrais de painJe voudrais du painPartitive = "de" + definite article. "Bread" (pain) is masculine, so "du" (de + le), not just "de".
Elle boit de l'eauElle boit de l'eau (or: Elle boit un verre d'eau)Water (eau) is feminine and starts with vowel: "de l'eau" (not "de la eau"). Correct!
Nous mangeons les saladesNous mangeons de la salade (or: des salades)Indefinite quantities need partitive. "Some salad" = "de la salade", not "les salades" (which means "the salads").

💬 Natural Conversation

Client: Bonjour ! Je voudrais du pain et une baguette, s'il vous plaît. (Hello! I'd like some bread and a baguette, please.)
Vendeur: Bien sûr. Et avec ça ? (Of course. Anything else?)
Client: Un café aussi, merci. (A coffee too, thanks.)
Vendeur: Voilà, ça fait cinq euros. (Here you go, that's five euros.)

Masculine and Feminine Nouns Overview

What are masculine and feminine nouns?

Every French noun is either masculine or feminine. The gender affects which article you use and how you form adjectives. Common patterns include:

  • Masculine nouns often end in consonants (le chien, le livre)
  • Feminine nouns often end in 'e' (la maison, la porte)
  • Always learn nouns with their articles to remember the gender

Nationality Adjectives — Feminine Formation Rules

How to form feminine nationality adjectives

Rule 1 (General): Add "e" to the masculine form
français → française, chinois → chinoise

Rule 2 (IEN/EEN endings): Change to "nne"
américain → américaine, coréen → coréenne

Rule 3 (Already ends in 'e'): No change
tchèque → tchèque, belge → belge

Liaison (linking sounds)

What is liaison?

Liaison is the pronunciation of a normally-silent consonant when the next word starts with a vowel or mute h. Examples:

  • un Américain — the "n" links to "Américain"
  • les Allemands — the "s" sounds like "z" (lez-Allemands)
  • les amis — liaison happens (lez-ami)
  • les villages — NO liaison (village starts with consonant)

Liaison creates smooth connections between words.

Prepositions Before Cities and Countries

Which preposition to use

  • à + city: à Toronto, à Paris
  • au + masculine country: au Canada, au Mexique
  • en + feminine or vowel-starting country: en France, en Angola
  • aux + plural country: aux Pays-Bas

Learn country genders individually—they're not always predictable.

Asking and Answering Nationality

How to ask and answer about nationality

Question: Quelle est votre/ta nationalité ? — What is your nationality?

Answers:

  • Je suis indien(ne). — I'm Indian.
  • Ma nationalité est indienne. — My nationality is Indian (always feminine as noun).
  • Je viens de l'Inde. — I'm from India.

Example Sentences

Je suis indien(ne). — I'm Indian.
Ma nationalité est indienne. — My nationality is Indian. (nationality is always feminine as a noun, so the adjective agrees as feminine regardless of the speaker's own gender)
Je viens de l'Inde. — I'm from India.
Je viens de la Côte d'Ivoire. — I'm from Ivory Coast.

Comprehensive Prepositions Guide

Prepositions by function:

PLACE: à (to/at), dans (in), sur (on), sous (under), devant (in front of), derrière (behind), entre (between), près de (near), loin de (far from), chez (at someone's home)

TIME: à (at specific hour), en (month/season), dans (future duration), depuis (starting point), pendant (duration), avant (before), après (after), jusqu'à (until)

CAUSE: à cause de (because of - negative), grâce à (thanks to - positive), en raison de (due to)

PURPOSE: pour + infinitif (to/in order to), afin de + infinitif (in order to - formal)

AFTER VERBS: penser à (think about), parler de (talk about), avoir besoin de (need), réussir à (manage to), essayer de (try to), commencer à (start to), arrêter de (stop)

❌ Common Preposition Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je vais en Paris.Je vais à Paris.Use "à" for cities, never "en". "En" is only for feminine countries.
Je vais au France.Je vais en France.France is feminine, so use "en" not "au". Masculine countries use "au".
Je pense de mon avenir.Je pense à mon avenir.The verb "penser" requires "à", not "de".
J'ai besoin à ton aide.J'ai besoin de ton aide."Avoir besoin" requires "de", not "à".
Il commence de travailler.Il commence à travailler."Commencer" requires "à" + infinitif, not "de".

Sam: Moi, je fais du sport avec des amis. (Me, I'm doing sports with friends.)
Julie: Amuse-toi bien ! (Have fun!)

Possessive Adjectives

Possessive Adjectives Overview

Possessive adjectives agree with the noun's gender and number, not the owner's gender:

  • Masculine singular: mon, ton, son, notre, votre, leur
  • Feminine singular: ma, ta, sa, notre, votre, leur
  • Plural (any gender): mes, tes, ses, nos, vos, leurs

Example: son stylo = his pen OR her pen (context tells you)

Key point: The possessive adjective matches the noun being owned, not the person who owns it. If the noun is masculine, use mon/ton/son, even if a woman owns it!

Important: Gender Agreement NOT Owner Agreement

🎯 Critical rule: Possessive agrees with the noun's gender, NOT the owner!

Example 1: A woman has a pen (stylo = masculine)

  • ✓ She says: mon stylo (masculine)
  • ✗ NOT: ma stylo (wrong!)

Example 2: A man has a house (maison = feminine)

  • ✓ He says: ma maison (feminine)
  • ✗ NOT: mon maison (wrong!)

Practice examples:

  • mon livre — my book (livre = masculine)
  • ma table — my table (table = feminine)
  • mon ami — my friend (ami = masculine)
  • ma chaise — my chair (chaise = feminine)
  • mes enfants — my children (plural)
  • mon frère — my brother (masculine, and note: frère ends in -e but is masculine!)
  • ma sœur — my sister (feminine)

Why this exception exists

Use masculine forms (mon, ton, son) before feminine nouns starting with a vowel or mute h—for smoother pronunciation:

  • ✓ mon amie (not ma amie) — my friend
  • ✓ ton amie (not ta amie) — your friend
  • ✓ son honnêteté (not sa honnêteté) — his/her honesty

Pronominal (Reflexive) Verbs

Structure of pronominal verbs

Pair subject + reflexive pronoun + verb:

  • je + me → je me parle
  • tu + te → tu te parles
  • il/elle + se → il/elle se parle
  • nous + nous → nous nous parlons
  • vous + vous → vous vous parlez
  • ils/elles + se → ils/elles se parlent

Note: me, te, se become m', t', s' before vowels.

SubjectReflexive pronounMeaning
jeme (m')myself
tute (t')yourself
il / ellese (s')himself / herself
nousnousourselves
vousvousyourselves
ils / ellesse (s')themselves

PronounConjugation

tut'appelles
il / elles'appelle
nousnous appelons
vousvous appelez

Laver vs Se Laver (Reflexive vs Non-Reflexive)

Same verb, different meanings

  • laver — to wash (something/someone): je lave la voiture
  • se laver — to wash (oneself): je me lave

The reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, etc.) changes the meaning by making the subject the object of the action.

laver (to wash — something)se laver (to wash — oneself)
je laveje me lave
tu lavestu te laves
il/elle laveil/elle se lave
nous lavonsnous nous lavons
vous lavezvous vous lavez
ils/elles laventils/elles se lavent

Daily Activities Vocabulary (from Professor's Lesson)

Morning routine:

Se réveiller — to wake up
Se lever — to get up / stand up
Se laver — to wash (oneself)
Se doucher — to take a shower (also: je prends une douche)
Se brosser — to brush (teeth, hair)
S'habiller — to get dressed

Throughout the day:

Prendre le petit-déjeuner — to have breakfast
Aller à l'école/au travail — to go to school / work
Assister à un cours — to attend a class
Travailler — to work
Prendre le déjeuner — to have lunch
Rentrer à la maison — to go back home

Evening routine:

Se reposer — to rest / relax
Préparer le dîner — to prepare dinner
Regarder la télévision — to watch TV
Faire ses devoirs — to do homework
Étudier — to study
Se coucher — to go to bed

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je laver meJe me laveReflexive pronoun comes BEFORE the verb, not after
Je me réveille à 7 heures (saying I wake up others)Je réveille les enfants à 7 heuresUse reflexive only when the action is done to yourself. Without "me", you wake someone else
Tu se lavesTu te lavesReflexive pronoun must agree with subject: "tu" uses "te", not "se"
Je doucheJe me doucheShower is reflexive (you shower yourself). Must use reflexive pronoun

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: Je me réveille à 7 heures tous les matins

I wake up at 7 o'clock every morning. Notice the reflexive pronoun "me" comes before the verb "réveille".

Example 2: Je me lave et je m'habille avant le petit-déjeuner

I wash myself and get dressed before breakfast. Two reflexive verbs in one sentence.

Example 3: Je me douche après le travail

I take a shower after work. Common way to express showering with reflexive verb.

Example 4: Je me repose le week-end

I rest/relax on the weekend. Shows reflexive verb for how you spend your time.

Example 5: Je me couche à 22 heures

I go to bed at 10 PM. Essential reflexive verb for describing your evening routine.

Léa: Moi je me lève à huit heures, j'aime dormir un peu plus. (I get up at eight, I like sleeping a bit more.)

Future Tense of First Group (ER) Verbs

How to form the future tense

Keep the infinitive + add: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont

  • tu habiteras — you will live

Je mangerai du riz aujourd'hui. — I will eat rice today.

Appeler in Future Tense (Doubled Consonant Rule)

The doubled consonant pattern

Appeler doubles 'l' throughout: j'appelle (present) and j'appellerai (future)

  • Future: j'appellerai, tu appelleras, il appellera
  • Present (comparison): j'appelle, tu appelles, il appelle

This doubling preserves the pronunciation of 'appel' with a short 'e'.

Demonstrative Adjectives (ce/cet/cette/ces)

Forms of demonstrative adjectives

Agree with gender and number of the noun:

  • ce — masculine singular (ce stylo)
  • cet — masculine singular + vowel/h (cet ami, cet homme)
  • cette — feminine singular (cette voiture, cette femme)
  • ces — plural any gender (ces stylos, ces valises)

Cet exists for smoother pronunciation with vowels and mute h.

cette femme — this woman
cette fille — this girl
cette maison — this house
cesplural (masc. or fem.)ces stylos — these pens
ces valises — these suitcases
ces amis — these friends
ces appareils — these devices
"Cet" exists purely for pronunciation — it links smoothly with a following vowel/h sound. Context tells you gender when the pronunciation is identical (e.g. "cet ami" for a male friend vs "cette amie" for a female friend sound similar when spoken).

Practice: Identifying the Correct Form

Choose the correct form:

  • ce canapé ✓ — this sofa (masculine consonant)
  • cet appareil ✓ — this device (masculine vowel)
  • cette maison ✓ — this house (feminine)
  • cette valise ✓ — this suitcase (feminine)
  • ces amis ✓ — these friends (plural)
  • cet étudiant ✓ — this student (masculine vowel)
  • cette femme ✓ — this woman (feminine)
  • ces stylos ✓ — these pens (plural)

Common mistake: Don't mix up "ce" with "cet" or "cette". Remember: ce=consonant, cet=vowel/h, cette=feminine!

C'est vs Il/Elle Est

When to use each form

  • c'est + article + noun: C'est un artiste. / C'est le quartier.
  • il est / elle est + adjective: Il est américain. / Elle est calme.

Key: c'est is followed by a noun (with article), while il/elle est is followed by an adjective.

C'est vs Il/Elle Est Reference Table

FormMeaningUsed for
c'estit is / this isfollowed by an article + noun (un/une/le/la + noun)
il est / elle esthe is / she isfollowed directly by an adjective or nationality

C'est un artiste. — This is an artist.
C'est une visite d'1 heure. — This is a one-hour visit.
C'est le quartier historique. — This is the historical neighborhood.
C'est la place du Capitole. — This is the Capitol place.
Il est américain. — He is American.
Elle est calme. — She is calm.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
ce livre rougece livre rouge (or: c'est un livre rouge)Demonstrative + adjective is fine. But don't confuse "ce" (this) with "se" (reflexive pronoun).
ces une fillecette fille (or: c'est une fille)"Ces" is plural only. For feminine singular, use "cette" not "ces".
ce étudiantcet étudiantMasculine + vowel = "cet" not "ce". "Étudiant" starts with vowel sound.
Il est un professeurIl est professeur (or: C'est un professeur)Profession after "être": NO article for just the job. Use "c'est + article" when emphasizing WHO he is.
C'est intelligenteElle est intelligente (or: C'est une fille intelligente)After c'est + adjective alone (no noun): use nom/article + noun. Or use "il est / elle est" + adjective.

💬 Natural Conversation

Marc: Dis, c'est qui cette femme là-bas ? (Hey, who's that woman over there?)
Julie: Ça, c'est ma tante, elle est médecin. (That's my aunt, she's a doctor.)
Marc: Et cet homme à côté d'elle ? (And that man next to her?)
Julie: C'est mon oncle. Viens, je te présente ! (That's my uncle. Come, I'll introduce you!)

Topic: Frequency words (jamais/souvent/toujours) and negation with ne...pas, plus ER verb quiz and DELF A1 exam format overview. (Numbers 70+ moved to Chapter 2.)

Frequency Words (la fréquence)

Main frequency words

  • jamais — never (zero frequency)
  • souvent — often (medium-high)
  • toujours — always (high)

Place them in sentences: Je vais souvent au musée. = I often go to the museum.

Negation: ne...pas and ne...jamais

Sandwich negation structure

Standard negation (ne...pas):
Je veux ce stylo → Je ne veux pas ce stylo (I don't want this pen)

Never negation (ne...jamais):
Je ne veux jamais ce stylo. (I never want this pen)
Je ne vais jamais au théâtre. (I never go to theater)

Jamais replaces pas for "never" in the same structure.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
soixante dix (without hyphen)soixante-dixFrench numbers use hyphens to connect compound numbers like 70.
quatre-vingt (for 81)quatre-vingt-un81 needs "un" after it. Don't use "et" here (that's only for 71).
Je ne veux pas jamaisJe ne veux jamaisDon't mix "ne...pas" with "ne...jamais". Use one or the other, not both.
Je veux pas ce styloJe ne veux pas ce styloIn formal French, you need "ne" before the verb in negation, not just "pas".
Je souvent vais au muséeJe vais souvent au muséeFrequency words go after the verb in simple present, not before.

💬 Natural Conversation

Tom: On va au restaurant ce soir ? (Shall we go to a restaurant tonight?)
Léa: Je ne mange jamais au restaurant en semaine, désolée. Je préfère cuisiner. (I never eat at restaurants on weekdays, sorry. I prefer to cook.)
Tom: Pas de problème, je viens chez toi alors ? (No problem, I'll come to your place then?)
Léa: Avec plaisir ! Mais je ne bois pas de café le soir, on prendra du thé. (Gladly! But I don't drink coffee in the evening, we'll have tea.)

Grammar: Asking "What time is it?"

Both mean the same thing — literal translation doesn't always work between languages (e.g. "fait" = "does," but this isn't about doing anything here).

Colors (les couleurs) with Gender Agreement

Color adjectives agree with the noun

Add 'e' for feminine: noir → noire, blanc → blanche, vert → verte, bleu → bleue, violet → violette

No change: rouge, rose, jaune, orange, marron (same in masculine and feminine)

Example: une voiture noire = a black car (feminine noun + feminine color)

Blacknoirnoire

Vocabulary: word-lookalikes with "vert/verre/vers"

Same or similar pronunciation, different meanings — context decides:
vert = green  |  un ver de terre = earthworm  |  un verre = a glass (drinking)  |  vers = towards
rouge à lèvres = lipstick (don't translate word-for-word: "red for lips")

The 5 Core Connectors

Five core connectors and their uses

  • pour — goal (followed by infinitive or noun)
  • parce que — cause (followed by subject + verb)
  • à cause de — because of (followed by noun only)
  • mais — but / opposition (followed by full clause)
  • avec — with / presence (noun/pronoun)
  • sans — without / absence (noun/pronoun)

Core Connectors Reference

ConnectorMeaningExpressesFollowed by
pourfor / in order tothe goalverb (infinitive) or noun
parce quebecausethe causefull clause (subject + verb + noun)
à cause debecause of / due tothe causenoun or pronoun only
maisbutoppositionfull clause
avecwithpresencenoun/pronoun
sanswithoutabsencenoun/pronoun
See Class 16 for more worked examples and the assignment correction on these same connectors.

Je vais au collège pour étudier. — I go to college to study.
L'Espagne a gagné parce qu'ils ont bien joué. — Spain won because they played well.
Je ne suis pas venu à cause de toi. — I didn't come because of you.
Il est drôle mais il est méchant. — He's funny but he's mean.
Je vais au magasin avec mon ami. — I go to the shop with my friend.
Je vais au magasin sans mon ami. — I go to the shop without my friend.

Pour + Infinitive

Pour always uses the infinitive

When pour is followed by a verb, use the infinitive (unconjugated) form:

  • Je vais au collège pour étudier. (I go to college to study.)
  • Il va au magasin pour acheter du pain. (He goes to the shop to buy bread.)

In English we use "-ing" (for studying), but French uses infinitive (pour étudier).

Present Continuous: "En Train De"

Two ways to express present continuous

Option 1: Simple present tense
J'étudie. = I study / I am studying.

Option 2: être + en train de + infinitive (more emphatic)
Je suis en train d'étudier. = I am (right now) studying.

The second option emphasizes an action in progress. Both are correct.

FrenchEnglish
je suis en train d'étudierI'm studying
je suis en train de laverI'm washing
je suis en train de mangerI'm eating

Grammar: Recognizing verb groups by infinitive ending

Corrected note: -er → 1st group (except aller), and -re/-oir → 3rd group, but not every -ir verb is 2nd group — many (partir, venir, ouvrir...) are irregular 3rd-group verbs instead. See Les Groupes de Verbes near the start of A1 for the full, correct rule (the "-issant test") and the complete breakdown.
The infinitive is the base/dictionary form of a verb, before it's conjugated for a subject (je, tu, il...).

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
une voiture rougeune voiture rouge (correct)Some colors (rouge, rose, jaune, orange, marron) never change form. They stay the same for masculine and feminine.
Je vais au musée pour mangerJe vais au musée pour voir l'art (or pour étudier)"Pour" uses infinitive, not conjugated verb. Be clear about the actual goal.
Je vais au magasin parce que je veux mangerJe vais au magasin parce que j'ai faim (or pour acheter du pain)"Parce que" gives the reason. "Pour" gives the goal/purpose — use the right one.
Je suis en train étudierJe suis en train d'étudier"En train de" requires "de" (de + verb = d'étudier when verb starts with vowel).
Il vient à cause il était maladeIl ne vient pas à cause de sa maladie"À cause de" requires a noun/pronoun only, not a full clause with subject + verb.

💬 Natural Conversation

Nina: Il est déjà cinq heures, on doit se dépêcher ! (It's already five, we need to hurry!)
Léo: Attends, je choisis une chemise. La bleue ou la verte ? (Wait, I'm choosing a shirt. The blue one or the green one?)
Nina: La bleue, clairement. Le vert ne te va pas. (The blue one, clearly. Green doesn't suit you.)
Léo: D'accord, la bleue alors ! (Okay, the blue one then!)

Pour + Infinitive (Detailed)

Pour always takes infinitive

Example: J'aime aller à la maison pour manger avant de retourner à l'école.
= I like to go home to eat before going back to school.

The verb after pour (manger) is in infinitive form.

Connectors: Parce Que vs À Cause De

Critical difference

parce que: + subject + verb (full clause)
L'Espagne a gagné parce qu'ils ont bien joué.
(Spain won because they played well.)

à cause de: + noun/pronoun only
Je ne suis pas venu à cause de toi.
(I didn't come because of you.)

They cannot be swapped—the structure must match!

Other Connectors

ConnectorUseExample
parce quebecause — followed by a full clause (subject + verb)L'Espagne a gagné parce qu'ils ont bien joué. (Spain won because they played well.)
à cause debecause of — followed by a noun or pronoun onlyJe ne suis pas venu à cause de toi. (I didn't come because of you.)
Rule of thumb: parce que = subject + verb (+ noun) follows. à cause de = only a noun/pronoun follows, no verb. They cannot be swapped.

Grammar: mais (opposition) / sans (without) / avec (with)

ConnectorMeaningExample
maisbut (opposition)J'ai une voiture mais je prends le bus. (I have a car but I take the bus.)
sanswithoutOn préfère le centre ville sans voiture. (We prefer downtown without a car.)
avecwithAvec ma femme, on prend le bus. (With my wife, we take the bus.)

Grammar: devoir — verb vs noun

Devoir as a verb = "to have to." Un devoir as a noun = "a task/homework/assignment."
Qu'est-ce que vous devez apporter? — What do you have to bring? (verb)
C'est un devoir. — It's a homework/task. (noun)

Compound words (mots composés)

Some word pairs combine into one meaning and shouldn't be translated word-for-word.
grands-parents = grandparents (not "big parents")
petit-déjeuner = breakfast (not "small lunch")

When minutes are "00," there are a few ways to say it:

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je vais au musée parce que j'aime l'artJe vais au musée pour voir l'art (or parce que j'aime l'art)Don't confuse "parce que" (reason/cause) with "pour" (purpose/goal). Both work but express different ideas.
À cause de il était malade, je ne viens pasÀ cause de sa maladie, je ne viens pas (or parce qu'il était malade...)"À cause de" needs only a noun/pronoun, never a full clause with subject + verb.
Je dois apporter du pain avec le dînerJe dois apporter du pain pour le dîner (or: Je dois apporter du pain au dîner)"Pour" = goal/purpose. "Avec" = with/together. Choose based on meaning.
sans vous, on reste à la maisonSans vous, on reste à la maison (correct)This is actually correct. "Sans" (without) takes only a noun/pronoun like "à cause de".
Il a un devoir à faireIl a un devoir à faire (correct — devoir = noun: homework/task)Be careful: "un devoir" (a task/homework) vs "devoir" (verb: to have to). Context determines the meaning.

Claire: Super, à huit heures alors ! (Great, eight o'clock then!)
Ami: J'ai hâte ! (Can't wait!)

Adjective Agreement (suivant/suivante)

Adjectives agree with noun gender

  • l'annonce suivante (feminine) — the following announcement
  • l'animal suivant (masculine) — the following animal
  • la voiture suivante (feminine) — the following car

Add 'e' for feminine; keep masculine form otherwise.

Grammar: quel vs qu'est-ce que

Quel = "which" or "what" — used with a noun. Example: Quel jour? (Which day?)
Qu'est-ce que = "what" — used when asking about an action/thing more generally. Example: Qu'est-ce que vous devez apporter? (What do you need to bring?)

Present Participle Rule: -ANT vs -ISSANT

The participle pattern

  • 1st and 3rd groups: -ANT ending (manger → mangeant, partir → partant)
  • 2nd group only: -ISSANT ending (finir → finissant, choisir → choisissant)

The -ISSANT ending is the unique marker for second group verbs!

VerbGroupPresent participle
aller — to goirregular (3rd)en allant
manger — to eat1sten mangeant
parler — to speak1sten parlant
marcher — to walk1sten marchant
partir — to leave3rdpartant
finir — to finish2ndfinissant
choisir — to choose2ndchoisissant

Grammar: Expressing an ongoing action

French has no direct "-ing" present continuous tense. Two ways to express it:
1) être en train de + infinitive — emphasizes the action is happening right now.
2) Simply use the present tense — often just as natural.

I'm going to school — je suis en train d'aller à l'école, or simply je vais à l'école.
She is finishing her homework — elle est en train de finir son devoir, or simply elle finit son devoir.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je vend la voitureJe vends la voitureVendre is 3rd group. Add 's' for je/tu: je vends, tu vends. The stem is "vend-" not "vend".
Il met sur la table le styloIl met le stylo sur la tablePrepositions of place typically come after the verb and object, not before.
Je finir le travailJe finis le travail (or: Je vais finir le travail)Finir is a 2nd group verb. Conjugate: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent.
Elle sont en train d'étudierElle est en train d'étudier (or: Elle étudie)"Elle" is singular, so use "est" not "sont". Use the correct conjugation of être.
À côté la maisonÀ côté de la maison"À côté de" (beside) requires "de" before the noun. Don't forget the preposition de.

💬 Natural Conversation

Client: Cette veste est jolie. Elle coûte combien ? (This jacket is nice. How much is it?)
Vendeur: Quinze euros. Je vous la mets dans un sac ? (Fifteen euros. Shall I put it in a bag for you?)

Conditional Tense (Le Conditionnel)

How to form the conditional

Future stem + endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient

  • Je mangerais — I would eat
  • Tu choisirais — You would choose
  • Il parlerait — He would speak

Special uses:
je devrais = I should
je pourrais = I could

Pronounmanger (1st group)choisir (2nd group)
jemangerais — I would eatchoisirais — I would choose
tumangerais — you would eatchoisirais — you would choose
il / ellemangerait — would eatchoisirait — would choose

vousmangeriez — you would eatchoisiriez — you would choose
ils / ellesmangeraient — they would eatchoisiraient — they would choose

Grammar: Should & Could

"Should" = devoir in the conditional. "Could" = pouvoir in the conditional — same future stem (devr-/pourr-) plus the conditional endings.
je devrais manger — I should eat.
je pourrais manger — I could eat.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je mangerai dans une heureJe vais manger dans une heure (or: Je mangerai dans une heure — future)Both work, but "aller + infinitive" (near future) is more natural for immediate future. Future tense is more formal.
en marchant à la maisonen marchant, je suis allé à la maisonGérondif ("en marchant") expresses "while" or "by" doing something, not the action after it.
Je vendrai mon voiture demainJe vendrai ma voiture demain (or: Je vais vendre ma voiture demain)Use "ma" (feminine possessive) with "voiture" (feminine noun), not "mon".
Je choissir le dessertJe choisis le dessert (or: Je vais choisir le dessert)Choisir is 2nd group. In present: je choisis (with double 's'), not "choissir". Future: je choisirai.
Je pourrai mangé du painJe pourrais manger du painAfter "pourrai" (future) or "pourrais" (conditional), use the infinitive form of the verb, not past participle.

Sam: Tu pourrais prendre une semaine le mois prochain, non ? (You could take a week off next month, right?)
Léa: Peut-être, si je finis ce projet à temps. (Maybe, if I finish this project in time.)
Sam: Je suis sûr que tu y arriveras ! (I'm sure you'll get there!)

📚 Learning Objectives

Grammar: Adjective Agreement

What is adjective agreement? Adjectives MUST change to match the noun's gender and number.

Why? French adjectives are grammatically linked to nouns — they describe them and must agree with them.

How? If the noun is feminine, add -e. If plural, add -s. These simple patterns apply to most adjectives.

Adjectives MUST AGREE with the noun in gender and number.

PatternMasculineFeminineExample
Basic + -egrandgrandeun grand garçon, une grande fille
Already -ecalmecalmeun enfant calme
-f → -veactifactiveun garçon actif, une fille active
-x → -seheureuxheureuseun homme heureux, une femme heureuse
-ien → -ienneancienancienneun ancien professeur, une ancienne maison
-on → -onnebonbonneun bon ami, une bonne idée
Irregularbeaubelleun beau jour, une belle maison
-if → -ivesportifsportiveun homme sportif, une femme sportive
-al → -aux (plural, masc.)nationalnationaleun jour national, des jours nationaux
Note: -al adjectives are unusual — the FEMININE follows the normal +e pattern (nationale), but the MASCULINE PLURAL changes to -aux instead of just adding -s (nationaux, not "nationals").

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
une grand amieune grande amieFeminine noun needs feminine adjective. Add -e to grand → grande
un active garçonun garçon actif"Garçon" is masculine, so use "actif" (not "active"). Feminine doesn't match
une femme heureuxune femme heureuseFeminine noun needs -se ending. "Heureux" → "heureuse" for feminine
les hommes bonles hommes bonsPlural needs -s. Plural masculine = "bons" (not "bon")

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: Elle est une grande professeure

Translation: She is a great teacher. (Feminine "grande" matches feminine noun "professeure")

Example 2: Les enfants heureux jouent ensemble

Translation: The happy children play together. (Plural "heureux" matches plural noun "enfants")

Example 3: C'est un beau jour calme

Translation: It's a beautiful, calm day. (Both "beau" and "calme" are masculine singular to match "jour")

Grammar: Adjective Placement

In French, adjective placement is a key skill. Most adjectives go AFTER the noun, but BAGS adjectives (Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size) go BEFORE the noun. Sometimes position changes meaning completely!

Most adjectives come AFTER the noun (colors, nationalities, shapes, descriptors):

une voiture rouge — a red car
un étudiant français — a French student
une table ronde — a round table

Some adjectives come BEFORE the noun (beauty, age, goodness, size):

un petit garçon — a small boy
une grande maison — a big house
un beau film — a beautiful movie

⚠️ Position can change meaning!

un ancien professeur — a former teacher
un professeur ancien — an old (elderly) teacher
un grand homme — a great man
un homme grand — a tall man

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
un bleu voitureune voiture bleueColors ALWAYS come after the noun
un ancien homme (old age)un homme ancienWhen position changes meaning, use context correctly
une française belle femmeune belle femme françaiseBeauty adjectives come before; nationality after
le interessant filmle film intéressantMost descriptive adjectives come after

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: C'est une petite maison bleue (It's a small blue house — size before noun, color after)

The adjective "petite" (small/beauty) comes first, while "bleue" (blue/color) comes after the noun.

Example 2: J'ai rencontré une jeune femme française (I met a young French woman — age before, nationality after)

Age adjectives (jeune) come before the noun; nationality adjectives (française) come after.

Example 3: C'est un ancien président (He's a former president — position = meaning!)

The adjective "ancien" BEFORE the noun means "former," but "un président ancien" would mean "an old/elderly president."

Example 4: Un grand homme est arrivé (A great man arrived — "grand" before = importance)

Position matters: "un grand homme" = a great man; "un homme grand" = a tall man.

Example 5: Elle a acheté une robe magnifique (She bought a magnificent dress)

Even though "magnifique" could describe beauty, long adjectives typically come after the noun in modern French.

Special: Adjectives Before Vowels

Three adjectives have special masculine forms before vowels: beau→bel, nouveau→nouvel, vieux→vieil. Use these forms only when the next word starts with a vowel or silent h. This makes pronunciation smoother.
Three adjectives have special masculine forms before vowels or silent H:
beau → bel (un bel homme)
nouveau → nouvel (un nouvel abonnement)
vieux → vieil (un vieil homme)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
un beau hommeun bel hommeUse bel before vowels in masculine form
un nouveau albumun nouvel albumUse nouvel before vowels in masculine form
un vieux arbreun vieil arbreUse vieil before vowels in masculine form
un bel voitureune belle voitureUse special forms only with masculine singular; voiture is feminine

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: C'est un bel homme intéressant (He's a beautiful interesting man — bel before homme)

Homme starts with a vowel, so use "bel" not "beau."

Example 2: J'ai un nouvel iPad (I have a new iPad — nouvel before iPad)

iPad starts with a vowel sound, so we use "nouvel" instead of "nouveau."

Example 3: Mon vieil ami habite en France (My old friend lives in France — vieil before ami)

Ami starts with a vowel, so we use "vieil" instead of "vieux."

Example 4: un bel oiseau bleu (a beautiful blue bird — bel before oiseau)

Oiseau starts with "o" (a vowel), so use "bel" not "beau."

Grammar: Epithète vs Attribut

Epithète = adjective directly with noun (un chat noir). Attribut = adjective after a linking verb like être (Le chat est noir). Some adjectives can be used both ways, while others can only be used one way.
TypeDefinitionExample
ÉpithèteAdjective directly with noun (no verb)un chat noir (a black cat)
AttributAdjective after linking verb (être, sembler, etc.)Le chat est noir (The cat is black)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Un aimable homme parleUn homme aimable parle"Aimable" can only be used as attribut with être; use as epithet with more common adjectives
Le garçon est petit et rusé chatLe garçon est petit et rusé OR un petit et rusé garçonDon't mix epithète and attribut; keep them consistent
une femme est blondeune femme blonde OR La femme est blondeUse epithète for description with indefinite article; attribut with definite article after être
le chat noir le garçonle chat noirEpithète modifies ONE noun only; don't use adjective alone

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1 (Épithète): J'ai vu un beau film hier (I saw a beautiful film yesterday — adjective directly with noun)

The adjective "beau" is placed directly before the noun "film" without any verb. This is epithète.

Example 2 (Attribut): Le film est beau (The film is beautiful — adjective after être)

The adjective "beau" comes after the linking verb "est." This is attribut.

Example 3 (Épithète): une femme intelligente et forte (an intelligent and strong woman — both adjectives with noun)

Both "intelligente" and "forte" are placed directly with the noun "femme." Both are epithètes.

Example 4 (Attribut): Cette femme semble malade (This woman seems sick — adjective after sembler)

The adjective "malade" comes after the linking verb "semble." This is attribut.

Example 5 (Both): Une fille heureuse (epithet) et elle est heureuse (attribut) (A happy girl and she is happy — same adjective both ways)

The word "heureuse" can be used as both epithète (directly with noun) and attribut (after être).
