Grammar: What is an Adverb? (Complete Definition)

Adverbs are invariable words (never change). They modify verbs (how?), adjectives (how much?), other adverbs (how much?), or whole sentences (what's your opinion?). This is the key difference from adjectives.

An adverb is an invariable word (NEVER CHANGES, no gender or number agreement) that modifies or clarifies:

  • A VERB — Describes HOW an action is done: Il parle lentement (How does he speak? Slowly)
  • An ADJECTIVE — Describes the DEGREE or INTENSITY: Il est très beau (How beautiful? Very)
  • Another ADVERB — Modifies another adverb: Il parle très lentement (How slowly? Very slowly)
  • The WHOLE SENTENCE — Expresses an opinion about the entire idea: Malheureusement, il a raté l'examen (Unfortunately, he failed the exam)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
une femme rapideElle court rapidementUse adjectives for nouns, adverbs for verbs/adjectives
un home lentementIl parle lentementAdverbs don't modify nouns; they modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs
Elle est très heureuxElle est très heureuseThe adjective after être must agree in gender/number, not the adverb
Il marche lentement bienIl marche bien lentementAdverb of manner (bien, lentement) comes directly after the verb

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: Il parle lentement (He speaks slowly — adverb modifies verb)

Lentement is an adverb describing HOW he speaks — it modifies the verb "parle."

Example 2: Il est très beau (He is very handsome — adverb modifies adjective)

Très is an adverb modifying the adjective "beau" — it tells us the DEGREE of handsomeness.

Example 3: Il parle très lentement (He speaks very slowly — adverb modifies adverb)

Très is an adverb modifying another adverb "lentement" — it tells us HOW slow the speaking is.

Example 4: Malheureusement, il a échoué (Unfortunately, he failed — adverb modifies whole sentence)

Malheureusement expresses an opinion about the entire sentence — it tells us the speaker's attitude.

🎯 CRITICAL DISTINCTION: Adjective vs Adverb

Adjectives modify NOUNS and CHANGE (gender/number). Adverbs modify VERBS/ADJECTIVES/ADVERBS/SENTENCES and are INVARIABLE. This is the most critical distinction in French grammar — don't confuse them!

⚠️ This is the most important concept! Many students confuse these. Use this test:

FeatureAdjectiveAdverb
Describes/ModifiesNOUNS ONLYVERBS, adjectives, adverbs, OR whole sentences
AgreementCHANGES (gender & number)INVARIABLE — never changes!
Example 1Un homme heureux (A happy man) — modifies "homme" (noun)Il sourit heureusement (He smiles happily) — modifies "sourit" (verb)
Example 2Une femme rapide (A fast woman) — describes nounElle court rapidement (She runs fast) — describes action
Rule of ThumbCan you add it directly to a noun?
✓ YES = adjective
✗ NO = adverb		Does it describe HOW something is done?
✓ YES = adverb
✗ NO = adjective

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Un homme heureusementUn homme heureuxCan't say "a happily man" — use adjective for nouns
Elle parle rapideElle parle rapidementAdverb (rapidement) modifies verbs, not adjective form
Un enfant lentement joueUn enfant lent joue lentementUse adjective (lent) for noun; adverb (lentement) for verb
Il est très heureusementIl est très heureuxAfter être, the adjective agrees; adverbs don't modify adjectives after être

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1 (Adjective): C'est une jolie fille (She's a pretty girl — adjective describes noun)

Jolie is an adjective that agrees with the feminine noun "fille."

Example 2 (Adverb): Elle chante joliment (She sings prettily — adverb describes verb)

Joliment is an adverb modifying the verb "chante" — it's invariable.

Example 3 (Adjective): C'est un homme intelligent (He's an intelligent man — adjective)

Intelligent agrees with the masculine noun "homme."

Example 4 (Adverb): Il parle intelligemment (He speaks intelligently — adverb)

Intelligemment modifies the verb "parle" and never changes.

Example 5 (Both): Une femme rapide court rapidement (A fast woman runs fast — both forms!)

Rapide (adjective) describes the woman; rapidement (adverb) describes how she runs.

❌ COMMON MISTAKE: Students try to use adverbs to modify nouns. WRONG!

❌ Un homme heureusement — INCORRECT (can't say "a happily man")
✓ Un homme heureux — CORRECT (a happy man) — adjective
✓ Il est heureux — CORRECT (He is happy) — adjective after linking verb
✓ Il sourit heureusement — CORRECT (He smiles happily) — adverb

Grammar: Complete Types of Adverbs (7 Categories)

7 adverb categories: Manner (how?), Time (when?), Place (where?), Frequency (how often?), Quantity/Intensity (how much?), Interrogative (question words), and Connectors (linking ideas). Each answers a different question — this is your key to mastering them!

1️⃣ Adverbs of MANNER — "Comment ?" (How is it done?)

Definition: These describe the WAY or MANNER in which an action is performed.

Key list (most common):

bien (well), mal (badly), lentement (slowly), rapidement (quickly), facilement (easily), sérieusement (seriously), poliment (politely), prudemment (carefully), paresseusement (lazily), prudemment (prudently)

Usage examples from class practice:

Il parle lentement (He speaks slowly) — describes HOW he speaks
Elle travaille beaucoup (She works a lot) — describes HOW MUCH she works
Je mange le gâteau doucement (I eat cake slowly) — describes HOW I eat
Elle conduit rapidement (She drives quickly) — describes HOW she drives
Il a bien travaillé (He worked well) — describes QUALITY of work

📚 Real-World Manner Examples

Example 1: Il parle couramment le français (He speaks French fluently — manner of speaking)

Couramment modifies how he speaks — describes the manner/style of speaking.

Example 2: Elle danse gracieusement (She dances gracefully — manner of dancing)

Gracieusement describes HOW she dances — the manner/style of her dancing.

Example 3: Je l'ai fait facilement (I did it easily — manner of doing)

Facilement describes the manner/ease of doing the task.

Example 4: Il a réussi brillamment (He succeeded brilliantly — manner of succeeding)

Brillamment describes HOW he succeeded — in a brilliant manner.

2️⃣ Adverbs of TIME — "Quand ?" (When?)

Definition: These indicate WHEN an action occurs or has occurred.

Extended list:

aujourd'hui (today), hier (yesterday), demain (tomorrow), avant-hier (day before yesterday), maintenant (now), bientôt (soon), déjà (already), récemment (recently), enfin (finally)

Real-life examples from class:

Aujourd'hui, je travaille (Today, I work) — starting the sentence
J'ai déjà mangé (I already ate) — between auxiliary & participle in passé composé
Il dîne toujours avant 19h (He always dines before 7 PM) — after verb
Je vais souvent au marché (I often go to the market) — after verb
Elle est toujours ponctuelle (She is always punctual) — modifying adjective

⚠️ IMPORTANT DISTINCTION:

tard — late (vague, no specific time reference). Example: Je mange tard (I eat late — no specific time)
en retard — late (after an expected/scheduled time). Example: Je suis en retard au travail (I'm late for work — after my usual time)

📚 Real-World Time Examples

Example 1: Hier, je suis allé au cinéma (Yesterday, I went to the movies — time adverb at start)

Hier indicates WHEN the action happened and starts the sentence for emphasis.

Example 2: Je l'ai déjà vu (I already saw it — short time adverb in passé composé)

Déjà is a short adverb that goes between the auxiliary and past participle in passé composé.

Example 3: Demain, je vais à la plage (Tomorrow, I'm going to the beach — future time)

Demain indicates WHEN the action will happen — a future time adverb.

Example 4: Récemment, j'ai vu un film intéressant (Recently, I saw an interesting film — recent past)

Récemment indicates the action happened recently — a past time reference.

3️⃣ Adverbs of PLACE — "Où ?" (Where?)

Definition: These indicate WHERE an action happens or WHERE something is located.

Complete list:

ici (here), là (there), là-bas (over there), ailleurs (elsewhere), partout (everywhere), nulle part (nowhere), dehors (outside), dedans (inside), devant (in front), derrière (behind), près (near), loin (far)

Classroom practice examples:

Les enfants jouent dehors (The children play outside) — describes WHERE they play
Il y a beaucoup d'invités dans la fête (There are many guests at the party) — WHERE the guests are
J'habite où ? — J'habite ici (Where do I live? — I live here) — location answer
Ma maison est près de la gare (My house is near the station) — position/location
Elle vient souvent ici (She comes here often) — WHERE she comes + FREQUENCY

📚 Real-World Place Examples

Example 1: Les enfants jouent dehors (The children play outside — location WHERE)

Dehors indicates WHERE the action happens — outside in the open air.

Example 2: J'habite ici (I live here — location WHERE)

Ici answers the question "Where do you live?" — a place adverb.

Example 3: L'école est près d'ici (The school is near here — relative position)

Près d'ici indicates a location relative to the speaker — near here.

Example 4: Partout où je vais, il y a du monde (Everywhere I go, there are people — location emphasis)

Partout indicates all places/everywhere — a comprehensive place adverb.

📖 Grammar: Formation of Adverbs of Manner (THE RULE)

The formation rule is simple: FEMININE ADJECTIVE + -ment = ADVERB. We use the feminine form because it usually has a vowel ending, making it easier to add -ment. Some adverbs like bien (well) and mal (badly) don't follow this pattern because they're independent words.

🔑 THE KEY RULE: Feminine Adjective + -ment = Adverb

To form most adverbs from adjectives, take the FEMININE FORM of the adjective and add -ment. This gives you the adverb.

WHY the feminine? Because it's a pattern: The feminine form often has a vowel sound at the end that makes it easy to add -ment.

MasculineFeminineAdverbMeaningExample
lentlentelentementslowlyIl parle lentement
rapiderapiderapidementquicklyElle court rapidement
heureuxheureuseheureusementhappily / fortunatelyHeureusement, personne n'a été blessé (Fortunately, nobody was hurt)
sérieuxsérieusesérieusementseriouslyElle a travaillé sérieusement
facilefacilefacilementeasilyOn peut le faire facilement
généralgénéralegénéralementgenerallyGénéralement, je vais au marché
actifactiveactivementactivelyIl participe activement
normalnormalenormalementnormallyNormalement, je dors 8 heures
habituelhabituellehabituellementusuallyHabituellement, elle arrive à 9h

💡 NOTE: Some adverbs don't follow this pattern. Bien (well) and mal (badly) are exceptions — they don't come from adjectives but are standalone adverbs.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Elle parle rapidement rapideElle parle rapidementThe adverb is the only form needed; don't use both adjective and adverb
Il est lent (for the adverb)Il parle lentementFor the adverb, use the feminine + -ment, not the masculine form
heurusementheureusementWatch spelling: heureux (masc) → heureuse (fem) → heureusement (adverb)
généralmentgénéralementDouble the -l- before -ment: général → générale → généralement

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1: Il parle lentement (He speaks slowly — from lent/lente)

lent (masculine) → lente (feminine) → lentement (adverb)

Example 2: Heureusement, il a réussi (Fortunately, he succeeded — from heureux/heureuse)

heureux (masc) → heureuse (fem) → heureusement (adverb)

Example 3: Elle travaille sérieusement (She works seriously — from sérieux/sérieuse)

sérieux (masc) → sérieuse (fem) → sérieusement (adverb)

Example 4: Généralement, je me lève tôt (Generally, I wake up early — from général/générale)

général (masc) → générale (fem) → généralement (adverb) — note the double -l-

Example 5: On peut le faire facilement (We can do it easily — from facile)

Note: facile doesn't change gender in French, so we just add -ment: facile → facilement

4️⃣ Adverbs of QUANTITY & INTENSITY — "À quel degré ?" (To what degree? How much?)

Definition: These indicate the AMOUNT or DEGREE of intensity of something.

Complete list:

très (very), trop (too much), assez (enough/quite), beaucoup (a lot/much), plus (more), moins (less), presque (almost), tellement (so much), vraiment (really), complètement (completely), à peine (barely)

Key examples showing usage:

Il est très grand (He is VERY tall) — modifying adjective, indicating degree
C'est trop difficile (It's TOO difficult) — showing excess
J'adore beaucoup ma famille (I LOVE a lot my family) — indicating amount of feeling
Nous sommes presque prêts (We are ALMOST ready) — nearly complete
C'est assez facile (It's QUITE easy) — sufficient degree
Il parle tellement (He speaks SO MUCH) — degree of action
C'est vraiment important (It's REALLY important) — emphasis on importance

⚠️ PLACEMENT RULE FOR QUANTITY/INTENSITY: These adverbs come BEFORE adjectives and adverbs, NOT after:

✓ Il est très beau (He is very handsome)
✗ Il est beau très — WRONG
✓ Elle parle très lentement (She speaks very slowly)
✗ Elle parle lentement très — WRONG

5️⃣ Adverbs of FREQUENCY — "Combien de fois ?" (How often?)

Definition: These indicate HOW OFTEN or HOW REGULARLY an action happens (frequency spectrum from always to never).

Frequency scale (most frequent → least frequent):

toujours (always) → souvent (often) → généralement (generally) → habituellement (usually) → normalement (normally) → parfois (sometimes) → rarement (rarely) → presque jamais (almost never) → jamais (never)

Real classroom practice examples:

Je vais souvent au marché (I go to the market OFTEN) — regularity of action
Elle est toujours ponctuelle (She is ALWAYS punctual) — consistent quality
Nous mangeons rarement au restaurant (We RARELY eat at restaurants) — infrequent action
Il ne fume jamais (He NEVER smokes) — zero frequency
Je dîne toujours avant 19h (I always have dinner before 7 PM) — consistent habit

⚠️ CRITICAL: "Jamais" as NEGATION ADVERB (NOT just frequency)

Jamais often pairs with ne to create negation in French. This is different from English "never" which stands alone:

Structure: ne + VERB + jamais (or ne + ADVERB + jamais)

Il ne fume jamais (He NEVER smokes) — negation of smoking
Je ne prends jamais le bus (I never take the bus) — negation of taking bus
Il n'a jamais visité la France (He has never visited France) — negation in past
Je ne mange jamais de viande (I never eat meat) — negation with partitive

⚠️ NOTE: Jamais CANNOT stand alone as a positive statement. Always needs ne for negation. Without ne, the meaning would be "ever" in questions.

6️⃣ Interrogative Adverbs — Question Words (Adverbes interrogatifs)

Definition: These adverbs are used to ASK QUESTIONS. They're the question words that ask about time, place, manner, reason, and quantity.

AdverbMeaningQuestion TypeExample
oùwherePlaceOù habites-tu ? (Where do you live?) → Answer: J'habite ici (I live here)
quandwhenTimeQuand arrives-tu ? (When are you arriving?) → Answer: Je arrive demain (I arrive tomorrow)
commenthowMannerComment ça va ? (How are you?) → Answer: Ça va bien (I'm doing well)
pourquoiwhyReasonPourquoi tu pleures ? (Why are you crying?) → Answer: Je suis triste (I'm sad)
combienhow much / how manyQuantityCombien ça coûte ? (How much does it cost?) → Answer: Ça coûte 10 euros (It costs 10 euros)

7️⃣ Linking Adverbs / CONNECTORS (Adverbes de liaison) — "Logical Connectors"

Definition: These adverbs CONNECT two sentences, ideas, or paragraphs. They help organize discourse and show relationships between ideas. VERY IMPORTANT FOR SPEAKING!

Note from class: Using logical connectors is essential for natural, organized French speech. It shows you're thinking clearly and organizing your ideas properly.

ConnectorFunction/UsageReal Classroom Examples
pourtanthowever, yet, still (shows contrast)Il courait. Pourtant, il est tombé. (He was running. Yet, he fell. — contrasts expectation)
cependanthowever, nevertheless (introduces opposite idea)Les téléphones sont bien pour les enfants. Cependant, il faut que les parents observent. (Phones are good for children. However, parents must monitor. — contrasts two points)
ainsithus, so, in this way (shows result)Ainsi, on continue... (Thus, we continue... — summarizes previous point)
ensuitethen, next (shows sequence/order)D'abord, on se dépêchait. Ensuite, on a raté le train. (First, we rushed. Then, we missed the train. — shows what happened next)
enfinfinally, at last (shows completion)On a essayé trois fois. Enfin, ça a marché ! (We tried three times. Finally, it worked! — shows resolution)
égalementalso, equally (adds information)Marie est venue. Son frère également. (Marie came. Her brother also. — adds equal information)
malheureusementunfortunately (shows negative outcome)Nous avons raté le train. Malheureusement, on a attendu 2h. (We missed the train. Unfortunately, we waited 2 hours. — shows negative consequence)
heureusementfortunately, thankfully (shows positive outcome)Il y a eu un accident. Heureusement, personne n'a été blessé. (There was an accident. Fortunately, nobody was hurt. — shows positive consequence)

💡 Teaching insight from class: Connectors are used to link 2 phrases, sentences, ideas, or paragraphs together. They organize your thoughts logically and make your speech flow naturally. Students who use these consistently sound much more fluent!

🎯 CRITICAL: Placement of Adverbs (THE MOST IMPORTANT SECTION)

Adverb placement depends on TENSE and ADVERB TYPE: Simple tenses = AFTER verb. Passé composé SHORT adverbs = between aux & participle. Passé composé LONG adverbs = after participle. Intensity adverbs = BEFORE adjectives. This is the most important rule!

This is where many students make mistakes! Adverb placement changes based on TENSE and ADVERB TYPE.

Context/TensePosition RuleExamples from Class
SIMPLE TENSE (Present, Future, Imperfect) — Regular Verbs Adverb comes AFTER the verb

Structure: Subject + Verb + ADVERB + Object		 Il parle lentement (He speaks slowly)
Elle travaille beaucoup (She works a lot)
Je voyage comment ? Je voyage rapidement (I travel quickly)
Il court très vite (He runs very fast)
PASSÉ COMPOSÉ — SHORT/FREQUENT Adverbs Adverb goes BETWEEN the auxiliary and past participle

Structure: Aux + ADVERB + Past Participle

Short common adverbs: déjà, bien, mal, souvent, toujours, enfin		 J'ai déjà mangé (I already ate)
Il a bien travaillé (He worked well)
Tu as déjà travaillé ? (Have you already worked?)
Elle a souvent visité ici (She often visited here)
Il a enfin réussi (He finally succeeded)
PASSÉ COMPOSÉ — LONG Adverbs (Manner) Adverb goes AFTER the past participle

Structure: Aux + Past Participle + ADVERB

Long adverbs: rapidement, lentement, facilement, sérieusement, prudemment, etc.		 Il a répondu rapidement (He answered quickly)
Elle a travaillé sérieusement (She worked seriously)
Il a conduit prudemment (He drove carefully)
Nous avons mangé rapidement (We ate quickly)
BEFORE AN ADJECTIVE Adverbs of DEGREE/INTENSITY go BEFORE the adjective

NEVER after. These modify the adjective's intensity.

Common: très, trop, assez, beaucoup, plus, moins, si, vraiment, complètement		 Il est très beau (He is VERY handsome)
✗ Il est beau très — WRONG
C'est trop difficile (It's TOO difficult)
C'est vraiment important (It's REALLY important)
C'est assez facile (It's QUITE easy)
C'est tellement beau (It's SO beautiful)
BEFORE ANOTHER ADVERB Short adverbs often BEFORE; Long adverbs AFTER

Structure (short): Short Adverb + Long Adverb
Structure (long): Subject + Verb + Long Adverb + Short Adverb

TRICK: Shorter = further to the left; Longer = further to the right		 Il parle très lentement (He speaks VERY slowly)
✗ Il parle lentement très — WRONG
Elle travaille assez rapidement (She works QUITE quickly)
Il court vraiment vite (He runs REALLY fast)
On parle parfois très lentement (We sometimes speak very slowly)
ADVERBS OF TIME/PLACE at SENTENCE START Can come at BEGINNING of sentence for emphasis

Structure: Adverb + comma + Subject + Verb

Common: Aujourd'hui, Hier, Demain, Maintenant, Ici, Là		 Aujourd'hui, je travaille (Today, I work)
Ici, il y a beaucoup de gens (Here, there are many people)
Demain, nous arrivons (Tomorrow, we arrive)
Maintenant, on continue (Now, we continue)
CONNECTORS (Liaison Adverbs) At BEGINNING of new sentence/clause, usually with comma

Structure: Connector, + New sentence

These link ideas between sentences		 Il courait. Pourtant, il est tombé. (He was running. Yet, he fell.)
Malheureusement, nous avons raté le train. (Unfortunately, we missed the train.)
Heureusement, personne n'a été blessé. (Fortunately, nobody was hurt.)
Cependant, il faut surveiller. (However, we must monitor.)

🔑 THE PLACEMENT TRICK (From class teaching):

For adverb placement, use this rule of thumb:

  • SHORTER adverbs: Tend to come closer to the VERB (in passé composé, between aux & participle)
  • LONGER adverbs: Tend to come FURTHER from the verb (after the whole verb phrase)
  • INTENSITY adverbs: ALWAYS before the adjective/adverb they modify

❌ Common Placement Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Il parle bien rapidementIl parle très rapidementUse short adverbs (bien, mal) between aux & participle in passé composé, not in simple tenses
Il est beau trèsIl est très beauINTENSITY adverbs (très, trop, assez) ALWAYS come BEFORE adjectives
Il a rapidement mangéIl a mangé rapidementLong manner adverbs go AFTER past participle, not before
Il a bien rapidement mangéIl a bien mangé rapidementShort adverb between aux & participle; long adverb after participle (if needed)

📚 Real-World French Examples

Example 1 (Simple tense): Je parle lentement (I speak slowly — adverb AFTER verb)

In present tense: Subject + Verb + ADVERB

Example 2 (Passé composé, short): J'ai déjà mangé (I already ate — short adverb BETWEEN aux & participle)

Déjà is a short common adverb, so it goes between the auxiliary and past participle.

Example 3 (Passé composé, long): Il a répondu rapidement (He answered quickly — long adverb AFTER participle)

Rapidement is a long manner adverb, so it goes AFTER the past participle.

Example 4 (Intensity before adjective): C'est très difficile (It's very difficult — TRÈS BEFORE adjective)

Intensity adverbs ALWAYS come before adjectives: très + difficile, not difficile + très.

Example 5 (Time adverb at start): Aujourd'hui, je ne travaille pas (Today, I'm not working — time adverb can start sentence)

Time and place adverbs often come at the beginning for emphasis or organization.

Example 6 (Connectors at start): Cependant, il faut surveiller (However, we must monitor — connector at beginning with comma)

Logical connectors start new sentences or clauses to link ideas.

⚠️ NUANCED DISTINCTIONS & CONFUSING PAIRS

Many students confuse: aussi (casual) vs également (formal), rater (YOU miss) vs manquer (THING is missing from you), tard (general late) vs en retard (scheduled time late), personne (nobody with ne) vs une personne (somebody). These are critical for sounding natural in French!

Distinction 1: "Aussi" vs "Également" (Also/Too)

Both mean "also" but have subtle differences in usage:

WordMeaningNuanceExample
aussialso, tooMore casual, general. Can mean "therefore" in older texts. Very common.Marie est venue. Son frère aussi. (Marie came. Her brother too.)
J'aime les films. Moi aussi. (I like films. Me too.)
égalementalso, equally, likewiseMore formal, more emphatic. Emphasizes equality or parallel ideas. Academic feel.Marie est venue. Son frère également. (Marie came. Her brother likewise.)
Les parents aussi, équilibre également important. (Parents also, balance equally important.)

Distinction 2: "Rater" vs "Manquer" (To miss) — CRITICAL DIFFERENCE!

This is a common mistake! These two verbs are NOT interchangeable. Different structures, different meanings:

VerbMeaning/UsageSubject of SentenceExamples
raterMiss an opportunity, bus, plane, OR fail an exam. The subject makes a mistake or fails.The PERSON who missed/failedJ'ai raté le bus (I MISSED the bus — I wasn't there in time)
Il a raté l'avion (He MISSED the flight)
J'ai raté l'examen (I FAILED the exam — I did poorly)
Il a raté son examen (He failed his test)
manquerMiss someone/something (person misses you; thing is absent). Shows absence or lack.What is MISSING or who is MISSED (often reversed in English)Tu me manques (I miss you — literally "You are missing from me")
Il manque du sel dans la sauce (Salt is missing in the sauce — salt is the subject)
Le Canada me manque (I miss Canada — Canada is missing from me)
Ma mère me manque (I miss my mother)

🔑 THE KEY DIFFERENCE:

  • Rater = YOU make a mistake, YOU fail, YOU don't get there in time
  • Manquer = Something is ABSENT, someone is NOT THERE (you miss them)

Distinction 3: "Personne" (Nobody) — Context Matters!

Same word, completely different meaning depending on context:

UsageMeaningFunctionExample
personne (alone in negation)nobody, no oneNegation with neIl ne vient jamais. Personne n'a été blessé. (Nobody was injured.)
Je ne vois personne (I see nobody)
une personne (with indefinite article)a person, somebodyPositive statementUne personne est arrivée (A person arrived)
Il y a une personne à la porte (There is someone at the door)
des personnes (plural)people, personsPositive pluralDes personnes ont téléphoné (Some people called)

Distinction 4: "Tarde" (Adverb of time)

Tard means "late" but WITHOUT a specific reference time. It's vague:

Je me couche tard (I go to bed late — no specific time, just generally late)

En retard means "late" with reference to an EXPECTED time — you're behind schedule:

Je suis en retard au travail (I'm late for work — after my usual arrival time)
Le bus est en retard (The bus is late — after its scheduled time)

💡 MEMORY TECHNIQUE FOR MASTERING ADVERBS (From Teacher's Method)

🔑 The Secret to Remembering Adverbs: ASK WHAT QUESTION THEY ANSWER!

Each adverb type answers a specific question. By remembering the question, you'll remember the adverb type and usage:

QuestionAdverb TypeExamples
Quand ? (When?)TIMEaujourd'hui, hier, demain, bientôt, maintenant, récemment
Où ? (Where?)PLACEici, là, dehors, près, loin, devant, derrière, partout
Comment ? (How?)MANNERbien, mal, lentement, rapidement, facilement, sérieusement
Combien de fois ? (How often?)FREQUENCYtoujours, souvent, généralement, parfois, rarement, jamais
À quel degré ? (To what degree?)QUANTITY/INTENSITYtrès, trop, assez, beaucoup, plus, moins, presque, vraiment

📋 PRACTICE TIPS (From Classroom Teaching)

✅ DO THIS:

  • Always learn adverbs IN COMPLETE SENTENCES, never isolated words. Your brain learns context, not just vocabulary.
  • Practice using adverbs actively in sentences you create. Say them out loud, write them down, use them in context.
  • For each adverb, ask yourself: "What question does it answer?" This becomes automatic with practice.
  • Pay attention to placement! Make sure your adverb is in the right position for the tense.
  • Use adverbs in conversations. Logical connectors (pourtant, cependant, etc.) make you sound fluent!

❌ DON'T DO THIS:

  • ❌ Don't memorize adverbs as lists without context
  • ❌ Don't put adverbs in wrong positions — placement matters!
  • ❌ Don't confuse rater/manquer or autre/également
  • ❌ Don't use adverbs to modify nouns (that's what adjectives do)
  • ❌ Don't forget that adverbs are INVARIABLE — they never change form

📚 Professor's Live Class Notes (Extended)

Adverbs of Place (Adverbes de Lieu) — Answering "Où ?"

Complete place adverb list: ici, là, là-bas, ailleurs, partout, nulle part, quelque part, dessus, dessous, dedans, dehors, devant, derrière, près, loin, autour

Classroom examples from student practice:

  • Les enfants jouent dehors — The children play outside
  • J'ai cherché partout — I searched everywhere
  • Il ne va nulle part — He goes nowhere
  • Le chat est dessous — The cat is underneath/below
  • Elle habite loin — She lives far away
  • Ma voiture est près du jardin — My car is near the garden
  • Il y a des arbres autour de la maison — There are trees around the house
  • J'oublie les clés quelque part — I forget the keys somewhere

Key reminder: All these adverbs answer the question "où ?" (where?) and help students locate things or describe where actions happen.

Adverbs of Quantity (Adverbes de Quantité) — Answering "À quel degré ?" (To what degree?)

Quantity adverb list: très, trop, assez, beaucoup, plus, moins, presque, tellement, vraiment, complètement, particulièrement

Classroom examples:

  • Elle est très intelligente — She is very intelligent
  • Il travaille beaucoup — He works a lot
  • C'est trop cher — It's too expensive
  • Nous sommes presque prêts — We're almost ready
  • Mon frère mange beaucoup — My brother eats a lot
  • Il y a beaucoup d'invités dans la fête — There are many guests at the party

Important note: These adverbs are often placed BEFORE adjectives: très beau (very beautiful), assez facile (fairly easy), trop difficile (too difficult). The pattern is: ADVERB + ADJECTIVE.

Adverbs of Frequency (Adverbes de Fréquence) — Answering "Combien de fois ?" (How often?)

Frequency scale (from most to least):

toujours → souvent → généralement → habituellement → normalement → parfois → quelquefois → rarement → presque jamais → jamais

Classroom examples:

  • Je vais souvent au marché — I often go to the market
  • Elle est toujours ponctuelle — She is always punctual
  • Nous mangeons rarement au restaurant — We rarely eat at restaurants
  • Il ne fume jamais — He never smokes (uses ne...jamais construction)
  • Je vais parfois courir le matin — I sometimes go running in the morning
  • Je dîne toujours avant 19h — I always have dinner before 7 PM
  • Je ne mange jamais de viande — I never eat meat

Critical rule: When using "jamais" in a negative sentence, use the structure "ne...jamais": Il ne fume jamais (He never smokes). The "ne" comes before the verb and "jamais" comes after.

Adverbs: Interrogative & Linking (Connectors)

Interrogative adverbs (question words): quand, comment, pourquoi, combien, où

Examples:

  • Où habites-tu ? — Where do you live?
  • Combien ça coûte ? — How much does it cost?
  • Quand arrives-tu ? — When are you arriving?
  • Comment vas-tu ? — How are you?
  • Pourquoi parles-tu ? — Why are you speaking?

Linking adverbs/connectors: pourtant, donc, ainsi, ensuite, enfin, également, cependant, malheureusement, heureusement

Function: These connect sentences and ideas to show relationships between them.

Examples from class:

  • Malheureusement, nous avons raté le train — Unfortunately, we missed the train
  • Il est tombé, cependant il a continué — He fell, however he continued
  • Fortunately, nobody was injured — Heureusement, personne n'a été blessée

Important in speech: Using linking adverbs/connectors makes you sound fluent and shows logical progression of ideas. These will be revisited under "logical connectors" later.

Vocabulary Clarifications from Class

1. Rater vs Manquer (Critical distinction!)

  • Rater — YOU miss/fail at something (subject does the failing)
    • J'ai raté le bus — I missed the bus (I was late, so I missed it)
    • J'ai raté l'avion — I missed the plane (I got late, didn't catch it)
    • Il a raté son examen — He failed his exam (He didn't pass it)
  • Manquer — Something is MISSING/ABSENT from you or you MISS someone (object does the missing)
    • Tu me manques — You miss me (You are missing to me)
    • Il manque du sel dans la sauce — Salt is missing in the sauce (Salt is absent from the sauce)
    • L'Inde me manque — I miss India (India is missing to me)
    • Le Canada me manque — I miss Canada (Canada is missing to me)

2. Personne (Double meaning!)

  • Personne alone = Nobody (in negative construction: Personne n'est venu = Nobody came)
  • Une personne = A person/Someone (Je connais une personne = I know a person)

3. Été (Past tense of être)

  • J'ai été, tu as été, il/elle a été, nous avons été, vous avez été, ils/elles ont été
  • This is the passé composé of être (to be)
  • We focus on present tense now; past tense will be covered more fully later

📚 Learning Objectives

Master all 6 preposition categories and their functions. Understand regional rules (à/en/au/aux for cities & countries). Learn context-dependent meanings (à can be place OR time). Practice using prepositions in complete sentences. Build fluency through real classroom examples.

🎯 DEFINING PREPOSITIONS

Definition: An invariable word that introduces a complement and establishes a relationship between sentence elements. Examples: Je vais à Paris (I go to Paris — preposition "à" shows destination).

A preposition is an invariable word (NEVER CHANGES) that shows the relationship between elements of a sentence:

  • PLACE: Je suis à l'école (I am at school — preposition "à" shows location)
  • TIME: Le cours commence à 8 heures (The class starts at 8 o'clock — preposition "à" shows time)
  • MEANS: Je vais au travail en bus (I go to work by bus — preposition "en" shows transportation method)
  • ORIGIN: Je viens de France (I come from France — preposition "de" shows origin)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je suis en l'écoleJe suis à l'écoleSchools use "à", not "en"
Je vais au FranceJe vais en FranceFeminine countries use "en", not "au"
Je travaille pendant trois ansJe travaille depuis trois ans"depuis" for ongoing action; "pendant" for completed duration
Devant = beforeDevant = in front of; Avant = before (time)Devant is position; avant is time

1️⃣ PRÉPOSITIONS DE LIEU (Prepositions of Place)

These show WHERE something is: à (at), dans (in/inside), sur (on), sous (under), devant (in front of), derrière (behind), chez (at someone's place), entre (between), parmi (among), près de (near), loin de (far from)

Place prepositions answer the question: OÙ ? (Where?)

chezat someone's placeJe suis chez moiI am at my place

près denearJ'habite près de l'universitéI live near the university
loin defar fromIl habite loin du centreHe lives far from the center

2️⃣ PRÉPOSITIONS DE TEMPS (Prepositions of Time)

These show WHEN something happens: à (at specific time), en (months/years/seasons), dans (future duration), depuis (ongoing from past to now), pendant (completed duration), pour (planned duration), avant (before time), après (after time)

Time prepositions answer the question: QUAND ? (When?)

3️⃣ SPECIAL RULE: À, EN, AU, AUX FOR CITIES & COUNTRIES

CITIES: Always use "à" (à Paris, à Lyon, à Montréal)
FEMININE COUNTRIES: Use "en" (en France, en Italie, en Iran)
MASCULINE COUNTRIES: Use "au" (au Canada, au Japon, au Mexique)
PLURAL COUNTRIES: Use "aux" (aux États-Unis, aux Philippines)

À cause de: because of (usually negative)

🔟 CONTRACTED FORMS (Prepositions + Articles)

Prepositions automatically combine with articles:
à + le = au | à + les = aux | de + le = du | de + les = des
But: à + la = à la | de + la = de la | à + l' = à l' | de + l' = de l'

de lade + la (no contraction)Je reviens de la gare (I come from the station)

Je suis depuis deux ans iciJe suis ici depuis deux ans"Depuis" goes AFTER the main verb phrase
Je pense de mon avenirJe pense à mon avenirPenser requires "à", not "de"

Il commence de travaillerIl commence à travaillerCommencer requires "à"
Elle est intéressée à ce posteElle est intéressée par ce posteIntéressé par = interested in a position/job

📝 B1-B2 ADVANCED PRACTICE SENTENCES

Despite difficulties: Malgré les difficultés, elle a continué à travailler (Despite the difficulties, she continued working)

Thanks to efforts: Grâce à ses efforts, il a obtenu de bons résultats (Thanks to his efforts, he achieved good results)

Due to traffic: En raison des embouteillages, nous sommes arrivés en retard (Due to traffic jams, we arrived late)

In order to improve: Je me suis inscrit à ce cours afin d'améliorer mon français (I enrolled in this course in order to improve my French)

Since arrival: Depuis son arrivée, beaucoup de choses ont changé (Since his/her arrival, many things have changed)

Working in company: Elle travaille dans cette entreprise depuis qu'elle a terminé ses études (She has worked in this company since she finished her studies)

🗣️ Prepositions + Stressed Pronouns

After ANY preposition (avec, pour, chez, sans, devant...), you cannot use je/tu/il/elle/nous/vous/ils/elles. You need the stressed pronoun set instead: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.
Subject pronounStressed pronounExample

tutoipour toi (for you)
illuichez lui (at his place)
elleelledevant elle (in front of her)
nousnousavec nous (with us)
vousvoussans vous (without you)
ilseuxchez eux (at their place)
ellesellespour elles (for them)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
avec jeavec moiSubject pronouns (je/tu/il...) can NEVER follow a preposition
chez ilchez luiUse the stressed pronoun "lui" after a preposition, not "il"

⚖️ Quantity + DE vs. the Partitive

After a specific QUANTITY (un kilo, 400 grammes, une bouteille, beaucoup, un peu), always use plain de — never du/de la/des — no matter the noun's gender.

400 grammes de fromage (400g of cheese — NOT "du fromage")
un kilo de tomates (a kilo of tomatoes)
une bouteille d'eau (a bottle of water)
beaucoup de lait (a lot of milk) vs. je bois du lait (I drink some milk — partitive, no specific amount)

A2: Prepositions — Cause, Purpose & Fixed Expressions — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: A follow-up preposition class — telling apart the ways to express cause (à cause de / parce que / grâce à / en raison de / faute de), expressing purpose, and the fixed verb/adjective + preposition expressions that have to be memorized.

0 / 9 done

1️⃣ MOYEN — Means (par, avec, en)

par = by / through (a channel): Je lui ai envoyé par e-mail (I sent it to them by email)
avec = with (the instrument used): Je coupe le pain avec un couteau (I cut the bread with a knife)
en = by (transport, preferred over par): Je vais au travail en bus (I go to work by bus)

All three can mean "by", but they're not interchangeable:

  • Tu lui as parlé par téléphone ? (Did you talk to them by phone?)
  • J'écris avec un stylo (I write with a pen)
  • Je vais en train / Je vais en voiture (I go by train / by car — en, not avec, for transport)

2️⃣ CAUSE — Telling the Five Apart

à cause de = because of (usually negative): Le match est annulé à cause de la pluie (the match is cancelled because of the rain)
parce que = because (neutral explanation, not blame): Je suis en retard parce que je me suis réveillé tard (I'm late because I woke up late)
grâce à = thanks to (positive cause): Grâce à son aide, j'ai réussi (thanks to his help, I succeeded)
en raison de = due to (neutral/formal): Le vol est retardé en raison du mauvais temps (the flight is delayed due to bad weather)
faute de = for lack of: Faute de temps, nous allons nous arrêter ici (for lack of time, we're going to stop here)

The key distinction the class kept coming back to: à cause de blames something for a negative result, while parce que is just explaining why, with no blame attached. Compare:

  • Je suis en retard à cause de l'embouteillage (I'm late because of the traffic — blaming the traffic)
  • Je suis en retard parce que je me suis réveillé tard (I'm late because I woke up late — just the reason)
  • Mon cours est annulé à cause du réseau (my class is cancelled because of the network)
  • Nous avons abandonné le projet faute d'argent (we gave up the project for lack of money)

3️⃣ BUT — Purpose

pour + infinitif: Je travaille pour gagner de l'argent (I work to earn money)
pour + nom: C'est un cadeau pour ma mère (it's a gift for my mother)
afin de + infinitif (more formal): Il étudie afin de réussir l'examen (he studies in order to pass the exam)
dans le but de + infinitif (more formal): Nous agissons dans le but de résoudre le problème (we act in order to solve the problem)
  • Je voyage pour aller au Canada (I travel to go to Canada)
  • Je prends un couteau pour couper la viande (I take a knife to cut the meat)
  • Je marche pour être en bonne santé (I walk to be healthy)

4️⃣ Verbs That Always Take a Specific Preposition

penser à = to think about: Je pense à mon avenir
parler de = to talk about: Nous parlons de notre projet
rêver de = to dream of: Elle rêve de voyager
s'intéresser à = to be interested in: Il s'intéresse à la politique
avoir besoin de = to need: J'ai besoin de ton aide
dépendre de = to depend on: Tout dépend de la situation
essayer de = to try to: J'essaie de comprendre
commencer à = to start to: Il commence à travailler
arrêter de = to stop doing: Elle a arrêté de fumer

avoir besoin de came up a lot in class — it's conjugated with avoir, so the person changes but the expression stays the same shape:

  • Il a besoin d'une voiture (he needs a car)
  • Nous avons besoin d'une maison (we need a house)
  • J'ai besoin d'apprendre le français (I need to learn French)
  • Appelez-moi si vous avez besoin de moi (call me if you need me)

5️⃣ Adjectives That Always Take a Specific Preposition

être fier de = proud of: Je suis fier de mon travail
être capable de = capable of: Elle est capable de le faire
être prêt à = ready to: Nous sommes prêts à partir
être intéressé par = interested in (note: par, not à): Il est intéressé par ce poste
être responsable de = responsible for: Elle est responsable du projet
être satisfait de = satisfied with: Je suis satisfait du résultat

Not an exhaustive list — the same pattern applies to être content de, être heureux de, and être fatigué de, among others.

6️⃣ Quick Review: Contracted Articles

Preposition + ArticleContracts toExample
à + leauJe vais au marché
à + lesauxJe parle aux étudiants
de + leduJe reviens du bureau
de + lesdesJe parle des problèmes
à/de + la, à/de + l'unchangedJe vais à la banque, Je reviens de l'université

Il commence de travaillerIl commence à travaillercommencer takes à, not de
Elle est intéressée à ce posteElle est intéressée par ce posteintéressé takes par, not à

A2: Le Passé Récent & Le Passé Composé — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: Two past tenses — le passé récent (something that just happened, venir de + infinitive) and le passé composé (a completed past action, auxiliary verb + past participle, with avoir or être). L'imparfait is a separate, later class.

0 / 8 done

1️⃣ LE PASSÉ RÉCENT — Something That Just Happened

Structure: Sujet + venir (présent) + de + infinitif
venir: je viens, tu viens, il/elle/on vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils/elles viennent
Example: Je viens de finir mon travail (I just finished my work)

Before a verb starting with a vowel, de elides to d':

  • Je viens de boire l'eau chaude (I just drank the hot water)
  • Il vient d'arriver (he just arrived)
  • Nous venons de voir sa femme (we just saw his wife)
  • Je viens de me lever (I just got up)
  • Vous venez de finir de manger (you just finished eating)
Watch out: Tu viens d'où ? is NOT passé récent — that "de" is the preposition "from" (where do you come from), not this structure. Passé récent always needs an infinitive after "venir de".

2️⃣ LE PASSÉ COMPOSÉ — What It Is

passé composé = auxiliaire (avoir or être) + participe passé.
A past participle is never used alone in this construction — it always needs the auxiliary verb.
passé simple (a different past tense) exists but is only used in books/writing, never in speech.

3️⃣ Forming the Past Participle

Verb typeRuleExample
Regular -ERremove -ER, add -émanger → mangé
Regular -IRremove -IR, add -ifinir → fini
Regular -REremove -RE, add -uvendre → vendu
venir, tenir, devenirirregular: end in -uvenir → venu
ouvrir, offrir, découvrir, recouvrir, souffririrregular: end in -ertouvrir → ouvert
Some -oir verbsunpredictable, learn individuallyvoir → vu, croire → cru
Beyond these patterns, irregular verbs have to be learned one at a time using a conjugation app — there's no single rule that covers all of them. Pick 2-3 irregular verbs a day and look up their past participle.

4️⃣ Passé Composé with AVOIR

avoir (présent): j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont
With avoir, the past participle does not agree in gender/number with the subject.
  • J'ai visité Paris (I visited Paris)
  • Nous avons donné un cadeau à mon ami (we gave a gift to my friend)
  • Elle a eu une idée (she had an idea)
  • Vous avez acheté un billet (you bought a ticket)
  • J'ai terminé ma réunion (I finished my meeting)
Common mix-up: Vous avez un billet (you HAVE a ticket — present tense) is not the same as Vous avez acheté un billet (you BOUGHT a ticket — passé composé, auxiliary + past participle).

5️⃣ Passé Composé with ÊTRE

être (présent): je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont
With être, the past participle does agree in gender/number with the subject.

The 16 "Doctor and Mrs. Vandertrump" verbs (DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP):

  • Devenir, Revenir, Monter, Rentrer, Sortir, Venir, Arriver, Naître, Descendre, Entrer, Retourner, Tomber, Rester, Aller, Mourir, Partir

Plus all pronominal/reflexive verbs: Je me lève → Je me suis levé (I got up).

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Mangé (alone, as a full sentence)J'ai mangéA past participle is never used without its auxiliary verb

This is the first of three classes on être-verb agreement. This one covers just the core rule — the next two cover special cases/reference and worked examples/mistakes. It assumes you already know from an earlier class that avoir verbs never agree, and that the 16 Dr & Mrs Vandertramp verbs (plus all pronominal verbs) use être instead.

1️⃣ The Four Agreement Forms

Feminine adds -e. Plural adds -s. The two rules combine independently.
SubjectRuleExample (aller)
Masculine singularno changeil est allé
Feminine singular+ eelle est allée
Masculine plural+ sils sont allés
Feminine plural+ eselles sont allées

2️⃣ Person-by-Person: Je / Tu / Il / Nous / Vous / Ils

Same rule, organized by subject pronoun instead of by category. Model verb: aller — swap in any other Dr & Mrs Vandertramp participle and the pattern is identical.

PersonMasculineFeminine
je (I)je suis alléje suis allée
tu (you, informal)tu es allétu es allée
il (he)il est allé—
elle (she)—elle est allée
nous (we)nous sommes allésnous sommes allées
vous (you, formal/plural)vous êtes allé (one man) / vous êtes allés (several men or mixed)vous êtes allée (one woman) / vous êtes allées (several women)
ils (they, masc./mixed)ils sont allés—
elles (they, all fem.)—elles sont allées
Vous is the only pronoun with four possible forms — it can mean one person (formal "you") or several people (plural "you"), and it can be masculine or feminine, so all four combinations exist: vous êtes allé / allée / allés / allées. Context tells you which one applies.

One example sentence per person, so you can hear each form used naturally:

  • Je suis allé au marché. (I went to the market — man speaking)
  • Je suis allée au marché. (I went to the market — woman speaking)
  • Tu es allé à l'école ? (Did you go to school? — asked to a man)
  • Tu es allée à l'école ? (Did you go to school? — asked to a woman)
  • Il est allé au cinéma. (He went to the movies)
  • Elle est allée au cinéma. (She went to the movies)
  • Nous sommes allés à Paris. (We went to Paris — men or a mixed group)
  • Nous sommes allées à Paris. (We went to Paris — all women)
  • Vous êtes allé au parc ? (Did you go to the park? — formal, to one man)
  • Vous êtes allées au parc ? (Did you go to the park? — to several women)
  • Ils sont allés au théâtre. (They went to the theater — men or a mixed group)
  • Elles sont allées au théâtre. (They went to the theater — all women)

0 / 4 done
This is the second of three classes on être-verb agreement. It assumes you already know the core rule from the previous class — La Règle de Base (the four agreement forms and the person-by-person view).

1️⃣ Mixed Groups & Named Subjects

A group with at least one man in it is always treated as masculine plural, even if every other person is a woman — masculine dominates in French for mixed groups:

  • Paul et Léa sont descendus du train (Paul and Léa got off the train — mixed group, masculine plural, +s only)
  • Marc et Sophie sont allés au marché (Marc and Sophie went to the market — mixed group)

A single name is treated like any other subject, by its own gender and number:

  • Léa est arrivée en retard (one female name → feminine singular)
  • Paul et Marc sont arrivés en retard (two male names → masculine plural)
  • Léa et Sophie sont arrivées en retard (two female names → feminine plural)

2️⃣ The Pronunciation Exception: mort / morte

Adding -e, -s, or -es to a past participle almost never changes its pronunciation — allé, allée, allés, allées all sound identical. Mourir is the exception worth remembering: in il est mort the final "t" is silent, but in elle est morte the added "-e" makes that "t" get pronounced out loud.
  • Il est mort en 2020 (the "t" is silent)
  • Elle est morte en 2003 (the "t" IS pronounced here)

A2: L'Imparfait — Formation & Usage de Base — Practice Worksheet

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: L'imparfait (the imperfect past tense) — formation from the present-tense "nous" stem, the one irregular stem (être), and ten worked examples covering habitual actions, descriptions, and an ongoing action interrupted by another.

0 / 4 done
L'imparfait is a different past tense from le passé composé (covered in earlier classes): passé composé is for a single completed action, l'imparfait is for a habitual action, a description, or an ongoing background action. A full side-by-side contrast between the two is coming in a future class — this one focuses on building l'imparfait correctly.

1️⃣ Formation: Nous-Stem + Endings

Base: présent "nous" form, minus -ons, plus: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient

Model verb manger: nous mangeons → stem mange-:

PersonForm
jeje mangeais
tutu mangeais
il / elleil/elle mangeait
nousnous mangions
vousvous mangiez
ils / ellesils/elles mangeaient
Spelling note: mangeons already has the soft-g "e" built in for the present tense. Before -ions/-iez (which start with "i"), that extra "e" is dropped: nous mangions, not "mangeions".

2️⃣ The One Irregular Stem: Être

Être's imparfait stem is ét- — NOT derived from its present-tense "nous" form (nous sommes would wrongly suggest "somm-"):

PersonForm
jej'étais
tutu étais
il / elleil/elle était
nousnous étions
vousvous étiez
ils / ellesils/elles étaient

Every other verb — even ones irregular in the present tense, like faire, avoir, prendre, vouloir, aller — still follows the normal rule: nous faisons → fais-, nous avons → av-, nous prenons → pren-, nous voulons → voul-, nous allons → all-.

3️⃣ Worked Examples From the Worksheet

Ten sentences from a class worksheet, solved — notice the three use-cases: a habitual past action, a description/state, or an ongoing background action:

  • Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Douala. (When I was little, I lived in Douala — a past state + a past habitual situation)
  • Tu faisais du sport tous les jours avant ? (Did you use to play sports every day? — habitual)
  • Elle avait les cheveux longs quand elle avait 10 ans. (She had long hair when she was 10 — description + state)
  • Nous mangions toujours à midi à la cantine. (We always used to eat at noon at the cafeteria — habitual)
  • Vous preniez le bus chaque matin ? (Did you used to take the bus every morning? — habitual)
  • Ils étaient très fatigués hier soir. (They were very tired last night — a description/state, not a single completed action)
  • Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. (It was raining when I went out — imparfait for the ongoing weather, passé composé for the single action that happened during it)
  • Je regardais la télé quand tu as appelé. (I was watching TV when you called — same pairing: ongoing imparfait action interrupted by a single passé composé action)
  • Nous voulions partir mais il faisait trop froid. (We wanted to leave but it was too cold — two simultaneous past states)
  • On allait à la plage tous les dimanches. (We used to go to the beach every Sunday — habitual)
Worth noticing now: sentences 7 and 8 pair l'imparfait (the ongoing background action) with le passé composé (the single action that interrupts it) in the same sentence — il pleuvait / je suis sorti, je regardais / tu as appelé. This is the single most common use of l'imparfait. A full side-by-side contrast of the two tenses is coming in a future class.

✅ Overall Mastery

Topic: Narrating a story by combining passé composé (events) and imparfait (background/description) together — the reported-speech "a dit que + imparfait" pattern, 9 new narration verbs, and a worked story from class.

This builds on the earlier passé composé classes and L'Imparfait — it assumes you already know how to form both tenses. This class is about using them together, the way a real story is actually told.

1️⃣ The Core Pattern: Events vs Background

Passé composé moves the story forward. Imparfait paints the background. Real narration mixes both.
A pattern that comes up constantly: reporting what someone said or was doing — a dit que / a demandé que / a expliqué pourquoi + imparfait for the ongoing action being reported.
  • La mère a dit qu'elle faisait un gâteau à l'ananas pour Alex. (The mother said she was making a pineapple cake for Alex — "a dit" = the single act of saying, passé composé; "faisait" = the ongoing action being described, imparfait)
  • Elle a entendu un bruit. (She heard a noise — just one thing that happened, passé composé alone, no imparfait needed)

2️⃣ New Vocabulary for Narration

FrenchEnglishPassé composé / imparfait example

être inquiet / inquièteto be worriedil était inquiet
tomberto fallil est tombé (être-verb)
direto say / tellil a dit
chercherto look foril cherchait
vouloirto wantil voulait
se souvenirto rememberil s'est souvenu
avoir confiance en quelqu'unto trust someonej'ai confiance en toi
laisserto leave (something) / letil a laissé

3️⃣ 💬 Worked Story From Class

A grandmother is making a pineapple cake for her grandson Alex, who gets caught taking €20 from her bag. Each sentence below is tagged with why it's passé composé or imparfait:

  • Le bruit était très fort. (description — imparfait)
  • Il est tombé par terre. (event — passé composé, être-verb)
  • Mamie était toujours inquiète. (ongoing emotional state — imparfait)
  • Le fils a dit à mamie de ne pas s'inquiéter. (event — passé composé)
  • Il a dit que c'était juste un cahier qui est tombé. (reported description + event, together)
  • Mamie a demandé ce qu'Alex cherchait. (asked + was looking for — the reporting pattern)
  • Alex a expliqué pourquoi il fouillait le sac de mamie. (explained + was rummaging — same pattern)
  • Alex voulait acheter quelque chose. (ongoing desire — imparfait)
  • Il s'est souvenu que sa mamie avait confiance en lui. (remembered + an ongoing trust — imparfait)
  • Il a laissé le sac. (event — passé composé)
  • Elle est allée dans sa chambre pour prendre ses lunettes. (event — passé composé, être-verb)
  • Il pensait à prendre l'argent, mais... (ongoing internal consideration, cut off by what happens next — imparfait)

4️⃣ TCF Speaking Tip: Avoid Repetition, Use Sequencing Connectors

Mentioned in class: when narrating out loud, use logical connectors to show the order of events instead of repeating the same word or just stringing sentences together with no link between them — it keeps your story moving and is specifically something TCF/TEF speaking tasks reward.
FrenchEnglish
d'abordfirst
ensuitenext / after that
puisthen
aprèsafterward
enfin / finalementfinally / in the end

Compare the same story without and with connectors:

  • ❌ La mère a fait un gâteau. Elle a entendu un bruit. Elle a trouvé Alex. Il a expliqué. (flat — no sense of sequence, sounds like a list)
  • ✓ D'abord, la mère a fait un gâteau. Ensuite, elle a entendu un bruit. Puis elle a trouvé Alex avec le sac. Enfin, il a expliqué ce qui s'était passé. (First, the mother made a cake. Then she heard a noise. Then she found Alex with the bag. Finally, he explained what had happened.)

Le COD : Complément d'Objet Direct — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: Identifying the complément d'objet direct (COD) — the part of a sentence that directly receives the verb's action — and telling it apart from the COI (indirect object, introduced by a preposition).

0 / 3 done
This is a sentence-structure concept, not a tense. It's the first step toward eventually using object pronouns like le/la/les (which replace a COD) — covered in detail, along with COI and its own pronouns, in the next chapter, Les Pronoms Compléments : COD et COI. This one is just about correctly identifying the COD.

1️⃣ What a COD Is

In a sentence with the basic shape subject + verb + object, the COD is the object — the part that directly receives the action of the verb.

FrenchLiteral receiver of the action
Elle lit un livre.un livre — the book is what's being read

2️⃣ How to Identify a COD — 3 Rules

  1. Answers qui ? (who?) or quoi ? (what?) right after the verb
  2. Has NO preposition in front of it
  3. Generally comes directly after the verb

Worked examples — ask "verb + qui/quoi?" and the answer is the COD:

SentenceQuestionCOD
Elle lit un livre.Elle lit quoi ?un livre
Nous parlons français.Nous parlons quoi ?français
Il regarde son frère.Il regarde qui ?son frère
Tu bois du jus.Tu bois quoi ?du jus
Elle regarde le miroir.Elle regarde quoi ?le miroir

3️⃣ NOT a COD — Spotting the COI (and Non-Objects)

If the complement is introduced by a preposition, it is never a COD — no matter how closely related it looks. Giveaway questions: à qui ?, de qui ?, à quoi ?, de quoi ?, avec qui ?, pour qui ? — all have a preposition baked in, which means COI, not COD.
SentenceQuestionVerdict
Il parle avec son ami.Il parle avec qui ?COI (avec = preposition), NOT a COD
Nous parlons de son père.Nous parlons de qui ?COI (de = preposition), NOT a COD
Ils sont dans la classe.—NO COD at all — "dans la classe" is a place phrase, not an object

Les Pronoms Relatifs : Qui, Que, Où — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: Relative pronouns qui (replaces the subject), que (replaces the direct object), and où (replaces a place or time) — joining two sentences into one, plus two practical tricks for choosing between them.

0 / 6 done
A relative pronoun joins two sentences into one, by replacing a noun that would otherwise be repeated. Without it: J'ai un ami. Mon ami habite à Paris. With it: J'ai un ami qui habite à Paris. (I have a friend who lives in Paris)

1️⃣ QUI — Replaces the Subject

Qui replaces the subject of the next clause. The word right after qui is always a verb, never another subject.

J'ai un ami qui habite à Paris. (I have a friend who lives in Paris — "qui" = "mon ami", the subject of "habite")
La fille qui parle est ma soeur. (The girl who is talking is my sister — "qui" = "la fille", the subject of "parle")

2️⃣ QUE — Replaces the Direct Object

Que (or qu' before a vowel) replaces the direct object of the next clause. The word right after que is always a new subject, then its own verb.

Le livre que je lis est intéressant. (The book that I'm reading is interesting — "que" = "le livre", the object of "lis"; "je" is a new subject right after "que")
Le film que nous avons vu était drôle. (The movie that we watched was funny — "que" = "le film", the object of "avons vu")

3️⃣ OÙ — Replaces a Place or a Time

Où replaces a place or a time. Same shape as "que" (new subject + verb after it), but only for places/times.

C'est la ville où j'habite. (It's the city where I live — place)
Le jour où je l'ai rencontré, il pleuvait. (The day I met him, it was raining — time, also "l'année où..." = "the year when...")

4️⃣ Two Tricks for Choosing Between Que and Où

TrickHow it worksExample
1. Preposition testPut the noun back in its original spot. Does it need a preposition (dans/à/sur/en) before it? Yes → où. No → que.je lis LE LIVRE (no preposition) → que. j'habite DANS la ville (needs "dans") → où.
2. "There" testCan you naturally add "y" or "là" (there)? Yes → où. No → que.j'habite là ✓ makes sense → où. je lis là ✗ doesn't make sense → que.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
J'ai un ami qui il habite à Paris.J'ai un ami qui habite à Paris."Qui" already IS the subject — never add another subject pronoun after it
Le livre qui je lis est intéressant.Le livre que je lis est intéressant.The book is the object of "lis", not the subject — needs "que", not "qui"
La ville que j'habite.La ville où j'habite."J'habite DANS la ville" needs a preposition → use "où", not "que"

Les Pronoms Y et EN — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: The pronouns Y (replaces à + place/thing) and EN (replaces de + thing, or a quantity with du/de la/des/un/une) — which fixed prepositions trigger each one, and correct word order including in the negative.

0 / 7 done
Y and EN replace a whole prepositional phrase so you don't have to repeat it. Both sit in the SAME position as object pronouns like le/la/les — right before the conjugated verb (or before the infinitive, if there is one).

1️⃣ Y — Replaces À + Place or Thing

Y replaces à + place/thing (or a place with dans/sur/chez). It means "there" or stands in for "about it".

Vas-tu à la cafétéria ? — Non, je n'y vais pas. (Are you going to the cafeteria? — No, I'm not going there)
As-tu réfléchi à ma proposition ? — Oui, j'y ai réfléchi. (Did you think about my proposal? — Yes, I thought about it)

2️⃣ EN — Replaces DE + Thing, or a Quantity

En replaces de + thing, or a noun with du/de la/des/un/une as a quantity.

As-tu apporté des enveloppes ? — Oui, j'en ai apporté. (Did you bring envelopes? — Yes, I brought some)
As-tu pris un café ? — Oui, j'en ai pris un. (Did you have a coffee? — Yes, I had one — "un" stays at the end when counting ONE of something)
Vous souvenez-vous de votre enfance ? — Oui, je m'en souviens. (Do you remember your childhood? — Yes, I remember it — "se souvenir DE")

3️⃣ The Quick Test: Find the Fixed Preposition

Verb patternExamplesPronoun
Fixed À-verbspenser à, aller à, réfléchir à, s'intéresser àY
Fixed DE-verbsparler de, se souvenir de, avoir besoin de, revenir deEN
Quantity word (du/de la/des/un/une)des enveloppes, un caféEN
Specific place after à/dans/sur/chezà la cafétéria, dans la boîteY

4️⃣ Word Order (Including the Negative)

Both Y and EN go directly before the conjugated verb in simple tenses, and directly before the auxiliary in passé composé. In the negative, ne...pas wraps around the whole pronoun+verb group.

J'y vais. / Je n'y vais pas.
J'en ai apporté. / Je n'en ai pas apporté.
Les bijoux sont-ils dans la boîte ? — Non, ils n'y sont pas.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je vais y.J'y vais.Y/EN go BEFORE the verb, not after — same rule as le/la/les
Je ne vais pas y.Je n'y vais pas."Ne...pas" wraps around the pronoun+verb group, not just the verb
As-tu pris un café ? — Oui, j'en ai pris. (missing "un")Oui, j'en ai pris un.When counting exactly ONE item, "un"/"une" stays at the end of the sentence
Avez-vous besoin de lait ? — Non, nous n'y avons pas besoin.Non, nous n'en avons pas besoin."Avoir besoin DE" is a DE-verb, so it takes EN, not Y

5️⃣ Y/EN With a Second Verb, Questions, and the Negative Again

With TWO verbs (aller/devoir/vouloir/pouvoir + infinitive), Y/EN go right before the INFINITIVE, not the first verb. In an inverted question, Y/EN stay attached to the verb they belong to, before the hyphen.

Je vais y manger. (I'm going to eat there — not "j'y vais manger")
Je dois y aller. (I have to go there)
Y vas-tu ? (Are you going there?) / En as-tu pris ? (Did you take some?)
Tu veux t'y habituer ? (Do you want to get used to it? — reflexive + infinitive: "t'y" stays together)

Negative "un/une" rule: when counting exactly ONE item, un/une stays at the end in a POSITIVE answer (j'en ai pris un) but DISAPPEARS completely in a NEGATIVE answer.

As-tu un stylo ? — Oui, j'en ai un. (Yes, I have one)
As-tu un stylo ? — Non, je n'en ai pas. (No, I don't have one — NOT "je n'en ai pas un")

Reflexive verb in the negative: ne goes before the reflexive pronoun, and the whole group (reflexive pronoun + y/en + verb) sits inside ne...pas.

Je m'y habitue. / Je ne m'y habitue pas. (I'm not getting used to it)

Sentence typeWhere Y/EN goesExample
Simple tenseBefore the verbj'y vais
Passé composéBefore the auxiliaryj'y ai réfléchi
Verb + infinitiveBefore the infinitiveje vais y manger
Inverted questionStays with its own verby vas-tu ?
Negativene...pas wraps the whole group; un/une disappearsje n'en ai pas
Tense-matching rule: your answer keeps the SAME tense as the question. If someone asks As-tu réfléchi à ma proposition ? (passé composé), answer in passé composé too: Oui, j'y ai réfléchi.

✅ Overall Mastery

Les Pronoms Compléments : COD et COI — Live Class Review

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: The pronouns that replace a COD (le/la/les) or a COI (lui/leur) so you don't have to repeat the noun — the full COI explanation promised in the earlier COD class, which pronoun set to use, word order, elision, and a brief look at using both together.

0 / 6 done
This builds directly on Le COD, an earlier class — it assumes you can already tell a COD apart from a COI. This class is about the pronouns that replace them.

1️⃣ Quick Recap: COD vs COI

CODCOI
Receives the actionDirectlyIndirectly — through a preposition
Answers the questionqui ? / quoi ?à qui ? / à quoi ? / de qui ? / de quoi ?
Preposition in front?NoYes (à, de, pour, avec, en, chez, sur...)
ExampleJe vois un film.Je parle à mon ami.

2️⃣ The Pronoun Sets

me, te, nous, vous are identical for COD and COI — they never change. Only the 3rd person differs: COD → le / la / les. COI → lui / leur (lui covers BOTH genders singular).
PersonCODCOI
me / te / nous / voussame for both — me, te, nous, vous
3rd singular, masculinelelui (same word for both genders)
3rd singular, femininela
3rd plural, any genderlesleur

Je vois Marie. → Je la vois. (la = Marie)
Il invite ses amis. → Il les invite. (les = ses amis, plural)
Elle téléphone à sa mère. → Elle lui téléphone. (lui = à sa mère — lui doesn't change for gender)
Nous parlons à nos amis. → Nous leur parlons. (leur = à nos amis, plural)

3️⃣ Word Order & Elision

The pronoun always goes directly before the conjugated verb — same position as y and en from the last class. Never after the verb, the way English sometimes does ("I see her" puts "her" after "see").

le and la shorten to l' before a verb starting with a vowel sound. les, lui, and leur never elide.

Paul achète la voiture. → Paul l'achète. (la + achète → l'achète)
Vous cherchez votre clé. → Vous la cherchez. (no vowel clash — no elision needed)

4️⃣ Choosing the Right Pronoun — the Preposition Test

Use the same COD/COI test, just to pick the pronoun instead of just naming the noun. The clearest example: the exact same verb, two different object types.

SentenceObject typePronoun version
Je parle français.no preposition → CODJe le parle.
Je parle à mon ami.preposition "à" → COIJe lui parle.

Same verb — parler — but a different pronoun each time, because the object's TYPE changed, not the verb.

🎁 Going Further (optional — not required to check off this class)

A sentence can have BOTH a COD and a COI, replaced together. The COD pronoun always comes first: Je lis le livre à mon enfant. → Je le lui lis. (le = le livre, lui = à mon enfant). Manoj donne la pomme à Sonia. → Manoj la lui donne. The instructor flagged this as advanced and secondary — the priority for now is choosing COD and COI pronouns correctly on their own.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je vois la.Je la vois.The pronoun goes BEFORE the verb, not after
Elle téléphone à sa mère. → Elle la téléphone.Elle lui téléphone."Téléphoner à" takes a preposition, so it's COI → lui, not COD → la
Paul la achète.Paul l'achète."La" must elide to "l'" before a vowel-starting verb
Nous parlons à nos amis. → Nous les parlons.Nous leur parlons."Parler à" is COI (preposition "à"), so it needs leur, not les
Coming in a future class: in passé composé with avoir, the past participle normally does NOT agree with anything — except when a COD pronoun (le/la/les) comes before the verb, in which case it DOES agree. That rule gets its own full class — not covered here yet.

📌 Grammar Reminder: Adjective Agreement

This is the same rule from Adjectives — applied now across all 274 words above. French adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number.

Masculine → Feminine (add -e, or an irregular change): petit → petite, intelligent → intelligente, heureux → heureuse, sérieux → sérieuse, beau → belle, nouveau → nouvelle, vieux → vieille, blanc → blanche.

Singular → Plural (usually add -s): un étudiant intelligent → des étudiants intelligents; une voiture rouge → des voitures rouges.

Useful sentence pattern — subject + être + adjective: Je suis fatigué. / Elle est fatiguée. / Nous sommes fatigués.
For objects — article + noun + adjective: une voiture rouge, un pantalon noir, une maison moderne.
🎯 TEF/DELF Tip: practice each adjective in masculine, feminine, and plural forms whenever possible — this builds vocabulary, gender agreement, plural agreement, and speaking fluency together, all at once.

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
une femme fatiguéune femme fatiguée"Femme" is feminine, so the adjective needs the feminine form — add -e
un homme heureuseun homme heureux"Homme" is masculine — don't use the feminine form on a masculine noun
des voitures rougedes voitures rougesPlural nouns need the plural adjective form too — add -s
Il est un gentil homme (as a description)Il est gentil. / C'est un homme gentil."Il est" takes the adjective directly, no article — "c'est" needs the article + noun

Four example verbs per pattern this time, to prove the ending pattern generalizes — not just one.

Personpartirsortirdormirsentir

5️⃣ Avoir & Être (the two essential irregulars)

These two don’t follow any of the four patterns above — they’re irregular and have to be memorized by sight. They’re also the two most-used verbs in the entire language, so there’s only one example each, not four — there’s nothing else quite like them to compare against.

Personavoirêtre
Jej'aije suis
Tutu astu es
Il / Elleil ail est
Nousnous avonsnous sommes
Vousvous avezvous êtes
Ils / Ellesils ontils sont
Watch out: partir, sortir, dormir, and sentir all end in -ir just like finir, but none of them take the -iss- endings (nous partons, not "nous partissons"). Run the -issant test from Les Groupes de Verbes if you're ever unsure: "en partissant" isn't a real word, so partir is 3rd group (irregular), not 2nd group.

A2: Choisir le Bon "WHAT" — Quoi / Que / Quel / Qu'est-ce que — Vocabulary Reference

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: How to choose the right French word for "what" — quoi (end of question / after a preposition), que (formal, before the verb, with inversion), quel/quelle/quels/quelles (before a noun, agrees like an adjective), and qu'est-ce que (the safe no-inversion default).

0 / 5 done
English has one word for "what" — French has four, and which one you need depends on the sentence's grammar, not on meaning.

1️⃣ QUOI — End of the Question, or After a Preposition

Quoi sits at the END of a casual, spoken question, or directly after a preposition like avec/de/à.

Tu fais quoi ? (What are you doing? — casual)
Avec quoi ? (With what?)
Quoi de neuf ? (What's new?)

2️⃣ QUE / QU' — Before the Verb, Formal, With Inversion

Que/Qu' goes right before the VERB, in a more formal register, and always triggers INVERSION (verb-subject).

Que fais-tu ? (What are you doing? — more formal than "tu fais quoi")
Qu'aimez-vous ? (What do you like?)

3️⃣ QUEL / QUELLE / QUELS / QUELLES — Before a Noun, Agrees Like an Adjective

Quel(le/s/les) sits directly BEFORE A NOUN and agrees with it in gender and number — it behaves like an adjective, not a pronoun.
FormAgreementExample
quelmasc. singularQuel livre ? (What book?)
quellefem. singularQuelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?)
quelsmasc. pluralQuels films aimes-tu ? (What movies do you like?)
quellesfem. pluralQuelles couleurs préfères-tu ? (What colors do you prefer?)

4️⃣ QU'EST-CE QUE — The Safe Everyday Default

Qu'est-ce que is the SAFEST option — no inversion needed, subject-verb order stays normal.

Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? (What are you doing? — same meaning as "tu fais quoi" / "que fais-tu", easiest to build under pressure)
Qu'est-ce que c'est ? (What is it?)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Quoi fais-tu ?Que fais-tu ?Quoi never starts a formal inverted question — use que/qu' there
Quel est-ce que c'est ?Qu'est-ce que c'est ?Quel needs a noun right after it; with no specific noun in mind, use qu'est-ce que
Quel heure est-il ?Quelle heure est-il ?"Heure" is feminine, so quel must agree: quelle

A2: Négation — Rien, Personne, Plus — Vocabulary Reference

Copy to Gemini for practicing

Topic: Three more negation patterns beyond ne...pas and ne...jamais (taught earlier) — ne...rien (nothing), ne...personne (nobody), and ne...plus (not anymore) — same sandwich structure, plus the one word-order exception for "personne" in passé composé.

0 / 4 done
This builds on Negation (ne...pas, ne...jamais) from an earlier class — same sandwich structure, just swapping the second half.

1️⃣ NE...RIEN — Nothing

ne...rien = nothing. Same sandwich: ne before the verb, rien after.

Je ne mange rien. (I'm not eating anything.)
Il ne fait rien le dimanche. (He does nothing on Sundays.)

2️⃣ NE...PERSONNE — Nobody

ne...personne = nobody / no one. ⚠️ In passé composé, personne goes AFTER the past participle, not wrapped around the auxiliary like the others.

Je ne vois personne. (I don't see anyone.)
Elle ne parle à personne. (She doesn't talk to anyone.)
Je n'ai vu personne. (I didn't see anyone. — NOT "je n'ai personne vu")

3️⃣ NE...PLUS — Not Anymore

ne...plus = not anymore / no longer — shows a stopped action.

Je ne fume plus. (I don't smoke anymore.)
Il n'habite plus ici. (He doesn't live here anymore.)

❌ Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ WRONG✓ CORRECTExplanation
Je ne mange pas rien.Je ne mange rien.Never combine ne...pas with another negative word — use one, not both
Je n'ai personne vu.Je n'ai vu personne."Personne" goes AFTER the past participle in passé composé, unlike rien/pas/jamais
Je ne fume jamais plus.Je ne fume plus.Don't stack two negative words — pick the one that matches the meaning
PatternMeaningPassé composé word order
ne...pasnotwraps the auxiliary
ne...jamaisneverwraps the auxiliary
ne...riennothingwraps the auxiliary
ne...plusnot anymorewraps the auxiliary
ne...personnenobodyAFTER the past participle (exception)
